ROAD ALLOWANCE
speechtext:
1.	Since January 1, 1956 have the members of the Saugeen Indian band voted upon a resolution to surrender a certain portion of their reserve land to the corporation of the county of Bruce, such land to be a road allowance of approximately seven miles in length?
2.	If so, and with respect to each such vote (a) upon what dates were they conducted? (b) how many members of the band were in attendance? (c) how many voted in the affirmative? (d) how many voted in the negative?
3.	What action, if any, has been taken to effect the surrender of the land?

speakeroldname: Mr. John Charlton (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: ROAD ALLOWANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in answer to question No. 208, there was no surrender of the roadway referred to in the hon. member's question. What we are concerned with here is not a formal surrender but a transfer of the land in question, which is technically quite a different matter under the Indian Act. The matter was considered at a band meeting on June 23, 1958 at which 65 electors were present. Forty agreed to make the land available, 16 voted against the proposal and the remainder declined to vote. On the same day the council of the band passed a resolution agreeing to a transfer of a 100-foot road allowance through Saugeen Indian reserve No. 29 without payment of compensation. This was all that was required under section 35 of the Indian Act, and the right of way for the road was conveyed to the province of Ontario by order in council.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a question to the Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton).
In looking over Monday's paper, I recognized a well known figure who is credited with an article entitled:
Hamilton-I have no sympathy for letter carriers who complain about salaries.
Does the Postmaster General care to make any comment on this statement and explain whether he intends to run his department by humiliating and provoking all his employees?
(Text):

speakerposition: Postmaster General
subtopic: POSTAL EMPLOYEES
subsubtopic: REPORTED DISSATISFACTION WITH RECENT SALARY INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I was in Halifax on Sunday a member of the press asked me about a press report that an official of the letter carriers association had said that they were most dissatisfied with their salaries and were considering strike action or a work stoppage. I said at that time, and I repeat, that I have no sympathy whatsoever for that sort of attitude. In my view it is unreasonable, unfair and irresponsible in the light of the conditions which exist today, because, with some 25,000 civil service employees in the department, substantial increases for well over half were announced early last month.
These increases were the largest ever announced in the history of the department. They averaged 12| per cent, while in the period since the last increase the cost of living index has gone up only 6J per cent. The result is that practically all those whose salaries were increased are now earning over $4,000 a year. I think that is exceptionally fair and reasonable treatment. Under these circumstances I think those who complain about salary treatment have no case whatsoever.
According to the report to which the hon. member referred, the association officials were complaining that the increases were not large enough and that certain classes had not yet been granted increases. My understanding of the situation is that the Minister of Finance announced several months ago that all salary classes would be reviewed, and that whatever salary increases were decided upon would be implemented as recommendations were received. With 150,000 employees in hundreds of classes, that process takes time, and there must always be those classes which will be reviewed first and those that will follow. The
Inquiries of the Ministry only alternative to this process is a general over-all increase of salaries at the same time, and to this the association itself has objected.
What the association which made the observations to which the hon. member refers were arguing for, and he can support them if he so desires, was that the government should not announce and approve increases as recommendations come forward but should hold all increases until they could be announced together. I do not believe that would be a popular policy, because it would hold up salary increases for many categories. I have confidence in the Minister of Finance and in the process of salary adjustments which is being followed at the present time. I understand that these association officials feel they must have some criticism to make, no matter how unreasonable they may be at times, but I do not believe their present criticisms are justified.

Mr. Chairman, last evening in speaking to this particular amendment the Prime Minister ranged far and wide over the bill and over the history of recent years. Among other things he chided some of us on this side for not having supported his efforts over the years to bring about a bill of this kind. That was not too easy to do during those years, because the Prime Minister's own views in regard to the nature of such a bill changed from year to year, and it was never quite certain at any one time what kind of bill or indeed what kind of idea for a bill of rights the Prime Minister had in mind.
The Prime Minister made great play last night about the attitude of the government to the universal declaration of rights which in one of its provisions, is the foundation of this amendment. Indeed, we admit that the words of this amendment are to be found in the universal declaration of human rights. The words of some of our other amendments come from that document as well. Indeed, the words of one of the provisions put forward by the government were originally taken, in substance at least, from the universal declaration of rights.
In discussing the background of this amendment last night the Prime Minister vigorously attacked the record of the previous government for having done nothing over the years in regard to this declaration. In doing so I claim that he misrepresented that record. Before this universal declaration was signed by the representative of the Canadian government in 1948 it was discussed at some length with the provinces, because there were matters in it which affected provincial jurisdiction. In this regard it is to be distinguished from a proposed international bill of rights which has been under discussion for many years and which could not have been accepted

by the government, as we saw it at that time, even if it had been up for acceptance, because as a bill it would have had some provisions which were outside the federal jurisdiction.
However, the declaration was discussed very widely, and it was signed. The Prime Minister has said more than once, and most recently last night, and he keeps on saying that the document never received consideration in this parliament. Perhaps the Prime Minister has forgotten that in two successive sessions in 1947 and 1948, this draft declaration of human rights was considered by a joint committee of the house and the Senate. It was carefully considered. I think there were 20 meetings held by this committee. The Prime Minister himself was a member of that committee. I have looked up the records of the committee and the records of attendance at its sittings as well. Therefore to say that this parliament never had an opportunity to consider that declaration of human rights is not in accordance with the facts.
The Prime Minister may also recall that in 1950 there was a Senate committee which went into the whole question of a bill of rights, including the declaration of rights, and that that Senate committee did not recommend a bill of rights because after taking a great deal of evidence it decided that was not the best course to follow. Incidentally, that committee was under the chairmanship of a man to whom the Prime Minister rightly paid great credit for his work in this field, Senator Roebuck. The committee decided that there should be something which in their view would be more suitable than a bill of rights, a declaration of Canadian rights. In that declaration they included rights dealing with social and economic matters.
Meanwhile, over all these years the declaration of human rights could have been brought before the House of Commons at any time during any session by the Prime Minister or any of his colleagues. There were various ways by which that could have been done. There were a number of supply motions, any one of which could have been used to bring this matter to the attention of the house. The Prime Minister, who now chides the government of that day for doing absolutely nothing, took no action of that kind, nor did any of his colleagues take action at that time.
The Prime Minister has also had three years during which he has been responsible for the government of this country. During any of the sessions throughout those three years this declaration could have been brought before the House of Commons and we could have been asked to support it if the Prime Minister were really so interested and anxious to have it done. That declaration 79951-0-471J
Human Rights
could have been included in this bill. Approval of it could have been given in this bill if the Prime Minister so desired. No move of that kind was made, although this bill has been under consideration by the government for the past two or three years. Therefore this indignation at this time, in 1960, that so little action was taken in parliament about this declaration of human rights strikes me as being a shade synthetic.
Last evening the Prime Minister expressed his satirical satisfaction at the great transformation which, so he claimed, had taken place in the attitude of this party with respect to the question of human rights. There has been quite a transformation in the Prime Minister's own attitude which may be seen if you read the debates of 1947 and the discussions of 1948 and those which took place subsequently in this house on the question of a bill of rights.
One indication, however, of a lack of transformation in the Prime Minister's attitude, of his lack of willingness now to put into this bill before us something which in those days, he put forward as most desirable, an indication of his apparent inability to do now what he then proposed to have done, is the refusal of the government to accept this very amendment. We are not asking the Prime Minister to change his mind in this regard; we are asking the Prime Minister to put in this bill what he claimed years ago and over the years should be done, namely to put some clauses in the bill of rights to deal with social matters.
So that it will be quite clear what I am talking about, I will repeat what the Prime Minister said in this house on May 16, 1947, when the question of a bill of rights was being discussed. This is what he said as reported at page 3152 of Hansard:
Those were the political freedoms that I would have placed in a bill of rights. In addition to those, there would, of course, be social freedoms, if I may call them such, assuring educational, property and social security rights.
We are giving the Prime Minister and the government an opportunity to do now in this bill what they claimed as far back as 1947 should be done. That is the nature of this amendment, and it will be the nature of subsequent amendments on this subject.

It will be recalled, as has been pointed out by the Leader of the Opposition himself, that at that time the Prime Minister's suggestion was also for the reference of such a bill to the Supreme Court of Canada to see just what the parliament of Canada could include properly in such a bill. In other words the Prime Minister recognized then, as he recognizes now, that a bill of rights on that basis would probably require a reference to see whether this field, and if so, how much in this field, should be included in a federal legislative enactment.
What has been made perfectly clear over and over again is that since assuming office, and on considering all the matters now applicable and the probability or possibility of obtaining provincial consent to that kind of enactment, we came to the conclusion that at the present time, as a first step, it would be better to offer a bill of rights confined exclusively to the federal field of legislative competence.
It is for that reason in part that the bill of rights has been drawn in its present form without any reference to, or inclusion of, that kind of subject matter.
There is no secret about that. We are not in the least hesitant to admit that this was our intention. Upon reflection our intention is to take this first step to set the federal house in order in the field of bills of rights, and then at the appropriate time to initiate discussions with the provinces to see what further steps can be taken to bring about a bill to rights which will cover the whole field of those rights which it is desired to have

included in a bill of rights applying to all jurisdictions in Canada. This is a perfectly simple explanation of why the present bill does not contain-and one good reason why it does not contain-the provisions the Prime Minister referred to in the quotation placed on the record.
Now, with regard to those provisions contained in the universal declaration of human rights which my hon. friends opposite are constantly urging us to incorporate in the bill, again what the Leader of the Opposition has just said establishes and confirms the soundness of our judgment in saying that they should not be incorporated in the present bill. He himself has pointed out that when that declaration was referred to a committee of parliament, the finding of the committee was that much which was contained in it had to do with the field of provincial legislative competence.
This confirms what I have been saying over and over again in this committee and what I said in the special committee. It was for that reason that my hon. friends opposite, when they formed the government, were so hesitant, to use the words used by the Leader of the Opposition, to submit it to parliament in any way; and when they did, what they did was to refer it to a parliamentary committee. They did not refer it for adoption by a formal resolution, as I recall. They were concerned because they recognized that it embraced things which are in the provincial field of jurisdiction.
That is one of the reasons I urged in the special committee, and I have been constantly urging here, that makes it undesirable and unsuitable to attempt to write into this federal bill of rights so many of the things which are contained in the universal declaration, because to do so would inevitably and inescapably take our bill of rights outside the federal field of competence and bring it into a field where it might well fail because the courts would hold that we are legislating with respect to matters which are assigned exclusively to the provinces. Certainly it would be held that we were legislating in most of those fields where the limits of our jurisdiction are by no means clear.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, what the Leader of the Opposition has just said in my submission confirms in two precise and important respects the soundness of the stand we have taken, that those provisions of the universal declaration are not suitable to be included in a bill of rights which is designed to be a bill entirely within the federal field of competence.

Mr. Chairman, the observations of the Minister of Justice reflect the contradiction between the position

taken by the Prime Minister and that taken by the hon. gentleman who has just spoken. The Minister of Justice, of course, passed over the suggestion made by the Prime Minister when he spoke about these matters, as the Leader of the Opposition pointed out a few moments ago. The then hon. member for Prince Albert had proposed that there should be included in a bill of rights the kind of social welfare objectives set out in the amendment before the committee at the present time, and if there were any doubt on the matter the Supreme Court of Canada should be asked, he proposed, for an advisory opinion under a reference provided for by the Supreme Court Act.
This course is not being followed by the government at the present time. If the government had any doubt whether those kinds of rights could be included, the Prime Minister had a very good precedent; that is the proposal which he himself made that the Supreme Court of Canada ought to be asked for an advisory opinion. Therefore the observations made by the Minister of Justice do not really touch the point because he assumes, as the Prime Minister has, that what we are asking for in this amendment is something clearly outside the competence of parliament. They are two observations that must be made in consequence.
In the first place, it is clear that the intention of parliament is not to touch on matters that are outside section 91 of the British North America Act; and to make that clear, notwithstanding statements made in the debate which will not be considered by the courts in interpretation, we have proposed in the preamble a clear qualification as to the federal powers. And, as I indicated last night, again so there will be no doubt we propose later on, in the operative part of the bill, to establish clearly by provisions to be incorporated that this act has only to do with matters that come within the federal competence.
But what I want to point out as to this particular amendment is that hon. gentlemen are assuming that the federal parliament has no power within section 91 to provide for social welfare legislation. Last night the Prime Minister spoke of our conversion, and then he went on to point out how happy he was at that process of association with ideas which he claims belong to him alone. We must not forget, of course, that the real author of this bill in its basic form is not the Prime Minister or the Minister of Justice but Mr. Driedger, who sits in front of the minister and who was referred to by the Minister of Justice as the author of the bill
Human Rights
in its original form. I am not making an announcement that is being made for the first time.
But while the Prime Minister says that this conversion has taken place, he will not forget that the very thing we are asking for in this amendment was in very large measure undertaken by the administration which he criticized last night. The social security provisions we now have in Canada, passed by this house, involving family allowances, old age pensions, old age security, old age assistance, blindness allowances, disability pensions, the veterans charter and unemployment insurance, are all measures placed on the statute books of Canada by a Liberal administration. So it lies in our mouths, having taken the initiative in this field, to urge the government to recognize the validity of the amendment and to provide this right within the limits set out in the constitution, so far as the division of powers is concerned.
So I would hope that with this explanation, and particularly that of the Leader of the Opposition, there can be no doubt. The Prime Minister, as the Leader of the Opposition said, had no doubt about the right to include this kind of provision in a bill of rights; and because it is now recognized that we have passed all these social measures in this house, to the extent that these measures are within the ambit of federal power, how can the government take the position that this right must not be included because it is outside the competence of parliament, when it is clearly within it? I would remind the Prime Minister of what he suggested when he proposed in 1950 or thereabouts-I forget the exact date-that parliament should pass an act even though it might be of doubtful constitutional value, which would provide an argument to the federal government in the matter of disallowance. Mr. Ilsley dealt with that point, and suggested that it would be politically immoral for parliament to pass something knowing it to be unconstitutional, just as it was politically wrong for the Bennett administration between 1930 and 1935 to pass acts which Mr. Bennett, great lawyer that he was, certainly must have known were ultra vires of the parliament of Canada.
But that is not what the Prime Minister had in mind. He had no such doubt when, as the Leader of the Opposition reminded us, he said on May 16, 1947, as found on page 3152 of Hansard:
Those were the political freedoms that I would have placed in a bill of rights. In addition to those, would, of course, be social freedoms-
These are the words of the Prime Minister.
-if I may call them such, assuring educational, property and social security rights.

Human Rights
We are not asking for educational or property rights, but we are asking in this amendment for the recognition of social security rights, and we are using as one of our arguments the very recommendation made to parliament by the Prime Minister. For these reasons and those stated by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont and the Leader of the Opposition, I would hope there would be a recognition by the government that in this, the twentieth century, when the character of our industrial society is such as to make it urgent on the part of authority to provide for the needy through measures of this kind, this should be done, and that there will be no hesitation in doing so. In the light of these reasons I ask the Prime Minister to accept this amendment.

A great deal of social security legislation was submitted. I have the various references here. There was a reference of the Natural Products Marketing Act. There was a reference of the question of legislative jurisdiction to enact the employment and social insurance act. Mr. Bennett brought in unemployment insurance, and that was submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada to determine whether or not parliament had the authority to pass such legislation, as were several other matters such as the weekly hours and industrial undertakings act, the limitation of hours act, and so on. I am not going through the entire ambit of those submissions.
However, I do point out this fact; that the Bennett government placed this legislation on the statute books, and when the King administration came into power the first thing they did was to submit the whole question to the Supreme Court of Canada to ascertain whether or not this beneficial legislation was within the legislative authority of parliament. At that time Mr. Bennett passed legislation which the courts subsequently decided was not within the legislative competence of parliament. The King administration appointed counsel, and it has never been denied that those counsel were directed not to argue in respect of the legislative competence of parliament to do these things but rather to take the reverse attitude.
I am going now to refer to the various statements I have made in this connection. My hon. friends opposite keep referring to what I stated on May 6, 1947, and I am going to read the entire reference to the suggestions I made at that time in connection with a bill of rights. On page 3152 of Hansard for that date we find this:
When this session opened I placed a resolution on the order paper; hut private members' days have been, to all intents and purposes, nonexistent this session, and the resolution will not

come up for discussion. I drafted a bill of rights in order to give a lead in this regard so that a committee would have something upon which to base discussion of the subject, but I did not introduce it because of my desire to secure joint action on the part of all parties in this house.
This was in 1947, and I did not endeavour to monopolize the subject, a position that could not be taken by any hon. member with a sense of responsibility, but tried to secure joint action and joint support. I continue the quotation:
This is not a political or partisan matter. It is one that, in order that success may be achieved, must have the support and co-operation of hon. members in all parts of this house and in the provinces of this dominion. The bill of rights I had drafted would have provided the assurance to Canadians, without regard to race or creed, of the following freedoms:
1.	Freedom of religion.
2.	Freedom of speech.
3.	Freedom of assembly.
4.	Freedom from wrongful interference by the state; and by that I mean freedom from unreasonable interference with person, home, reputation, activities and property of the individual.
5.	Freedom from arbitrary detention and in particular that habeas corpus shall not be suspended or abrogated except by parliament.
6.	The right of everyone to have his case determined without undue delay and assuring everyone required to give evidence before any tribunal or commission the preservation of all constitutional safeguards and, above all, the right of the individual to be represented by counsel. ..
7.	The right of equal protection for all against arbitrary discrimination in the provisions and applications of law because of race, religion or any other reason.
It was 13 years ago that these suggestions made in paragraphs 1 to 7 were outlined, and today they are embodied in this bill of rights, so there has not been any change of attitude. Then I went on to say this:
Those were the political freedoms that I would have placed in a bill of rights. In addition to those, there would, of course, be social freedoms, if I may call them such, assuring educational, property and social security rights.
Education is exclusively within the jurisdiction of the provinces, and property within a province is exclusively within the jurisdiction of the province. Then I went on to advocate that there should be a submission to the Supreme Court of Canada

Just let me conclude this point, and then I will give an answer. In 1952, on March 24, at page 714, I moved a resolution and I should like again to point out the elements of that resolution. It reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, immediate consideration should be given to the advisability of introducing a bill or declaration of rights to assure amongst other rights:
1.	Freedom of religion, freedom of speech, freedom of the press and of radio:
Human Rights
Today radio is not included, because since then freedom of the press has been defined as including freedom of the means of expression through the instrumentality of the radio. I continue to read:
2.	That habeas corpus shall not be abrogated or suspended except by parliament;
3.	That no one shall be deprived of liberty or property without due process of law, and in no case by order in council;
4.	That no tribunal or commission shall have the power to compel the giving of evidence by anyone who is denied counsel or other constitutional safeguards.
Then I said this as part of that motion:
And that as a preliminary step the government should consider the advisability of submitting for the opinion of the Supreme Court of Canada the question as to the degree to which fundamental freedoms of religion, speech and of the press and the preservation of the constitutional rights of the individual are matters of federal or provincial jurisdiction.
There was a considerable amount of discussion on this motion, and finally Mr. Harris, then the minister of citizenship and immigration, moved the adjournment of the debate. He pointed out that the minister of justice was most anxious to take part in that debate, and the result was that the yeas and nays were called and with the government members voting solidly, the matter was blocked so far as that session was concerned.
I am not going to review all the other examples of similar motions which I moved on other occasions. In other words, sir, everything that is embodied today in the bill of rights now before this committee was, in general and even in particular, advocated by me throughout the years in the form of motions and amendments. I even went further than that and on March 24, 1952, moved a motion which I think I ought to place on the record as well in order to answer the arguments which are being advanced. On that date, after introducing the resolution, I decided to bring before the house a draft declaration. I did that at page 719 of Hansard for that year, and I think it is well to have this recorded. It reads:
I have been asked what terms would be put into a bill of rights or into a declaration of freedom. I realize the difficulties of draftsmanship. Those who drafted the first ten amendments to the United States constitution took several years. Since that time we have had an example in the difficulty of the United Nations. Incidentally some three years ago a declaration of human freedoms was agreed on but as yet has not been brought before parliament. In the representations made to the committee in the other place, which committee was presided over with distinction by Senator Roebuck, some recommendations as to terms were made. I shall read a draft declaration of rights which I believe represents, in general, most of the principles to be embodied in such a bill of rights.
I have used as a base the draft declaration from the Senate committee, and have altered, added to or deleted some of its terms. I suggest

Human Rights
these as a basis upon which Canadians might consider the drafting of a Canadian bill of rights or declaration of rights:
Article 1
Everyone has the right to life, liberty and the security of person.
Article 2
No one shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
Article 3
Everyone has the right to recognition throughout Canada as a person before the law.
Article 4
All are equal before the law and are entitled without any discrimination to equal protection of the law.
Article 5
Everyone has the right to an effective remedy by the competent national tribunals for acts violating the fundamental rights granted him by the constitution or by law.
Article 6
(1)	No person shall be subjected to arbitrary arrest, detention or exile.
(2)	Any person who is arrested or detained shall be promptly informed of the reasons for the arrest or detention and be entitled to a fair hearing within a reasonable time or to release.
(3)	No one shall be denied the right to reasonable bail without just cause.
(4)	No tribunal, royal commission, board or state official shall have the right to compel anyone to give evidence who is denied counsel or other constitutional safeguards.
Article 7
Every person who is deprived of his liberty by arrest or detention shall have an effective remedy in the nature of habeas corpus by which the lawfulness of his detention shall be decided speedily by a court and his release ordered if the detention is not lawful. Habeas corpus shall not be abridged, suspended or abrogated except by parliament.
Article 8
Everyone is entitled in full equality to a fair and public hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal, in the determination of his rights and obligations and of any criminal charge against him.
Article 9
Every person is entitled to all the rights and freedoms herein set forth without distinction of any kind such as race, colour, sex, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, property, birth or other status.
Article 10
Any person whose rights or freedoms as herein set forth have been violated may apply for relief on notice of motion to the supreme or superior court of the province in which the violation occurred.
Finally article 11, and these were all of the articles:
Article 11
The above articles shall not be deemed to abridge or exclude any rights or freedoms to which any person is otherwise entitled.
I simply point out this fact, that the suggested bills of rights that I brought before the house covered those political and constitutional rights. In so far as the rights of

education or property within the province were concerned, those were matters which would naturally be included in any bill of rights national in scope, providing the provinces were willing to abrogate or permit any control over their exclusive jurisdiction in this regard.
I simply point out that fact, and I have nothing to withdraw through those years in what I advanced to the house; for all the things that are embodied in those successive resolutions, motions or draft bills of rights are today embodied in the one now before the house.

Then I perused Hansard of recent years and noted the references therein to this question which has been of interest to this house for a number of years, in which debates the Prime Minister and other members have taken an active part. and we have always stood for these principles, whether we were in office or out of office.
We in this group intend to support this amendment in all sincerity, because our conscience is clear as to what we have said and done in the years gone by.

As an example, I should like to show that the New Zealand bill of rights contains the following clause which I wish to quote, namely article 22 of the universal declaration of human rights, which is fully particularized and which is an example for our own bill of rights:
"Everyone, as a member of society, has the right to social security and is entitled to realization through national effort and international co-operation and in accordance with the organization and resources of each state, of the economic, social and cultural rights indispensable for his dignity and the free development of his personality."
This right is intimately associated with other provisions of the declaration-provisions which affirm the right to an adequate standard of living, to education, to choice of employment, and to rest and leisure. The question which the hon. member for Cartier has raised is, of course, a very important one, but it is a question in reply to which I know the hon. member would not expect me to be as completely categorical as the terms of his question might seem to require.
The phrase "freedom of religion" is a phrase which has been dealt with by the Supreme Court of Canada, in the Saumur case specifically, and it is a phrase which to my mind connotes the right of a person to worship God in his own way and in accordance with his own conscience. If he does not happen to be one who shares the religious beliefs of the majority in the existence and supremacy of God, he may yet worship whatever supreme being he does believe in in his own way and in accordance with the dictates of his own conscience. This freedom exists to everyone provided that in exercising that right, that freedom, he does not improperly interfere with the rights and freedoms of other people. That is, I think, all I can say.
If any individual feels himself aggrieved in or deprived of that freedom, or unduly limited or prescribed in the exercise of that freedom which, of course, he must exercise in accordance with the law, then he has the right of recourse to the courts, which have dealt with the matter in the Saumur case, and the courts will decide whether his freedom has been improperly abridged.

I want to deal now with clause 2, and in connection with that clause something which is perhaps legally the most important matter before us.
This bill, declaratory in form, is alleged by some proponents as having the effect of abrogating any existing measures inconsistent with the bill of rights. I have contended, as have other members-and I am not aware that there has been serious dispute concerning this statement-that to the extent this bill goes it is acceptable, but it is unacceptable because it does not abrogate legislation that is inconsistent with it.

Human Rights
The minister argued that the whole of clause 2 had the effect of a legal enactment. That was disputed by some members of the committee and by most of the witnesses who appeared before it, in particular Mr. David Mundell. If we are going to have a bill of rights, we in this Liberal party contend that we should have an effective bill of rights; one that has teeth in it; one that really will protect human rights and fundamental freedoms, and one that will be more than merely declaratory in consequence. We want a bill of rights that will see to it that any inconsistent legislation, which violates any of the provisions of the bill, will be inoperative.
We were referred by many hon. members on second reading to the Immigration Act, to the Lord's Day Act, to the Juvenile Delinquents Act, to the narcotic and drug control act and to other measures which are inconsistent with this bill and which will not cease to be operative in law by the mere passage of this bill in its present form. This was the view taken by the Canadian Bar Association, and by witnesses before the committee. This, of course, was the view taken by Mr. Bora Laskin, who unfortunately was not available as a witness but whose argumentation is so clear as to have warranted the support of all who commented upon it. For these reasons I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rose-mont:
That lines 11 to 18 be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"The interpretation act is amended by adding thereto under the heading of "rules of construction" immediately before section 9 thereof, the following section as section 8(A).
'8(A) 1. Every act of the parliament of Canada and every order, rule and regulation thereunder in force at the commencement of this section, and all laws in Canada that are subject to be repealed, abolished or altered by the parliament of Canada in force at the commencement of this section, are hereby amended by repealing or revoking them to the extent that any provision thereof would abrogate, abridge, or authorize the abrogration, abridgement or infringement of any of the rights or freedoms declared to exist in Canada by the Canadian bill of rights.'
'2. No act of the parliament of Canada, passed hereafter, shall, unless it is otherwise expressly stated in it be interpreted to abrogate, abridge or infringe, or to authorize the abrogation, abridgement or infringement of any of the rights or freedoms declared to exist in Canada by the Canadian bill of rights.'
'3. No act, order, rule or regulation or law mentioned in subsection 1, and, unless it is expressly otherwise stated therein, no act hereafter passed, shall be construed or have effect to.' "
Then we deal with the various clauses in the bill. We are face to face with an opportunity of testing exactly how far the government wants to go with this bill. If this bill is passed in its present form, we will be giving to the courts a wide opportunity of judicial

legislation, something that we should not do as a legislative body. Our function as a legislature is always to keep within our competence those matters, which are of a legislative character and to the courts we should give only the barest minimum opportunity of judicial law making. That is inherent in our whole system of government.
If we do not accept this amendment or one like it we will be doing what the Canadian Bar Association said we would be doing, that is giving an opportunity for an immeasurable amount of litigation as a result of the uncertainties which will be created. If this bill passes in its present form without this kind of amendment, there will be all sorts of legislation, inconsistent with this bill and which will have to come before parliament at some time, as well as many regulations and orders, all of them inconsistent.
There will be a task imposed on the Minister of Justice and the law officers of the crown the like of which will never have been placed on the Department of Justice. All that can be removed by making it clear in this bill that all acts now in existence and inconsistent with this measure are hereby abrogated. That is what is done in the amendment I have put forward. This is a vital matter.
There is standing in my name on the order paper a proposed amendment to the Expropriation Act. This amendment would cover that. If this bill pases in its present form the Expropriation Act will continue untouched as an abridgment-as it now is-of human rights and fundamental freedom, sought to be protected by this parliament.
Because this matter is important, I should like to refer the committee to what the Canadian Bar Association said on the matter, when Mr. Donald Mclnnes, dominion vice-president of the Canadian Bar Association and a very distinguished lawyer from Halifax, appeared before the committee. Beginning at the bottom of page 10 of Mr. Mclnnes' brief we find these words:
These questions point up the major problem of Interpretation Involved in section 3 of the proposed bill, which sets out rules of construction for legislation enacted by the parliament of Canada or under its authority.
I wish the minister would find it convenient to follow this, because this is really the heart of the whole matter.

Specific questions such as these illustrate the uncertainty about existing law to which section 3 of the bill gives rise. If Bill No. C-79 is enacted these and many other questions must be answered by the courts. There will be great latitude for judicial law-making. Lawyers generally oppose granting wide discretion to those who must apply the law, even the granting of discretion to our judiciary, for which we have the highest regard. I submit that this statement by the Canadian Bar Association has to be fully considered. I would remind the committee that this statement by the association was supported by Mr. F. A. Brewin, a distinguished lawyer from Toronto, who will be known to the hon. member for Port Arthur, and this should arouse his sympathy, interest and support. We now have a provision in clause 2 which we are considering which reads as follows:
Every law of Canada shall, unless it is expressly declared by an act of the parliament of Canada that it shall operate notwithstanding the bill of rights, be so construed and applied as not to abrogate, abridge or infringe or to authorize the abrogation, abridgment or infringement of any of the rights or freedoms herein recognized and declared, and in particular, no law of Canada shall be construed or applied so as to-
Then follow the subsequent words of clause 2. So it is now clear, even if it was not clear before, that this bill of rights operates as a law, as a rule of construction with respect to every statute of Canada, every law of Canada, unless that law of Canada expressly provides that it shall operate notwithstanding the bill of rights. Nothing could be clearer and nothing, in my opinion, could be more all-embracing; so that all that my hon. friend's amendment does in this respect is to take the protection which we seek to confer by the bill of rights out of the bill of rights and put it in the Interpretation Act, but it is nothing more than a rule of construction as he has drawn his amendment.
I was saying that it is a rule of construction, but it is a rule that he would transfer to the Interpretation Act instead of being left in the bill of rights. If my hon. friend seeks to hinge or to hang any particular argument on his use of the words "hereby amended by repealing or revoking them to the extent that any provision thereof would abrogate, abridge, or authorize the abrogation, abridgment" and so forth, I point out to him that that is a matter for interpretation and construction by the courts.
My hon. friend has not specified the acts which he says would be repealed or with respect to which he says certain provisions would be repealed or revoked by his amendment. The courts would have to interpret the acts that might come before them exactly as they would have to interpret the acts which would come before them by virtue of the provisions now contained in the bill of rights, and they would have to interpret those acts in the light of the words of the bill of rights to decide for themselves whether or not the provisions before them do operate so as to abridge, infringe, or authorize the abrogation, abridgment or infringement of any of the rights or freedoms herein recognized and declared.
Let me suggest to hon. gentlemen opposite that if we were ourselves to embark upon a program of revision of the statutes, for example, to see what specific provisions of which

statutes were contrary to the bill of rights, no one could say what specific provisions were or were not actually repealed in whole or in part by the proposed amendments, any more than he could say what statutes would be affected by our present wording. It is only when the enactment comes before the courts that the court acts in accordance with the rule of interpretation laid down, whether it be in the bill of rights or in the proposed amendment, and decides whether or not the statute operates in such a way that it would be contrary to the bill of rights.
Now, what is the position if the courts say that? They find an express legislative enactment of this parliament, as our bill is drawn, which says that every law of Canada shall, unless it is expressly declared by the parliament of Canada that it shall operate notwithstanding the bill of rights, be so construed and applied as not to abrogate, abridge or infringe. They will then have a look at the section or provision in question and say first, does this statute have within it an express declaration that it operates notwithstanding the bill of rights? If the answer to that question be no, it does not contain such an express provision, they would then look at the question of whether or not the provision of the statute which is before them does contravene the bill of rights. If the answer to that question be yes, then they would say, by virtue of the bill of rights we are directed not to give that statute or provision that construction, interpretation or application; in fact, we are directed not to apply it in a manner which will contravene the bill of rights.
Therefore the effect of the provision in our bill of rights is exactly the same as the effect of the provision in the proposed amendment, because under the proposed amendment the courts would have to go through exactly the same process. They would have to say first, is there an express provision in the statute before us that it operates notwithstanding the bill of rights? If the answer to that is no they would then say, Very well, we must then look at it to see whether or not the statute before us contains any provision which operates contrary to the bill of rights. If the answer to that question be yes, they would then interpret this section of the Interpretation Act embraced in the amendment in such a way as to have the effect of repealing or revoking the provisions of the statute before them.
So the process the courts would have to go through is exactly the same. They would have to interpret the statute before them from the point of view of whether or not it contains provisions that are contrary to the bill of rights and, if they found that it did, then by virtue of our bill of rights they would say, We are instructed not to apply

it in that way and accordingly we will not so apply it. If the only provision were the amendment now before us they would have to say, Well, this amendment says that we shall regard this provision of this statute as having been revoked or repealed.
In effect there is no difference whatsoever in the situation under the two alternatives with respect to the process that the courts would have to go through. The protection ultimately rests with the courts and the interpretation they give and the decision they reach as to whether or not the statute then before them contains or does not contain a provision contrary to the bill of rights.
I have said there would be no difference with respect to the process through which the courts would have to go, but there are important differences with respect to ancillary effects of this amendment. One of the most important is that it takes the protection we desire to give out of the bill of rights and puts it in the Interpretation Act. To my mind this is an undesirable effect. We want the bill of rights to be complete and to speak completely with regard to the rights of Canadians and the protection of those rights, and with regard to the instruction, the rule of interpretation, that shall be given to the courts in their application and protection of these rights. We do not want them to be scattered around by transferring them to the Interpretation Act. That would make the bill of rights an incomplete document, and we attach very great importance to enacting a bill of rights as a complete document.
I am not surprised that my hon. friends would seek to take this out of the bill of rights and put it in the Interpretation Act. They have been attacking the bill of rights indirectly all along.

You would weaken the protection that is afforded to the rights of the individual, not just because you would have taken it out of the bill of rights and put it into another statute, which I think in a very proper sense could be described as of lesser importance, but because you would have put it in a statute that parliament would have much less hesitation in amending than it would in amending or overriding the bill of rights. After all, all you would have to say before parliament if you wanted to take away these rights, indirectly and by subterfuge and concealment, would be that it was simply an amendment to the Interpretation Act. I think it is fair to say that probably only lawyers would be interested then. They would be mainly concerned because interpretation acts are understood to be mainly matters of legal import, which are of a technical nature and of concern to lawyers.
But the bill of rights is a statute about which all Canadians will know and whose effects will be dear to their hearts. As a result they will scrutinize any change most carefully and, I believe, from the point of view of being suspicious about what any government tries to do subsequently with the bill of rights. Therefore I am surprised again that my hon. friends, who have placed before us time after time proposals that would weaken the bill of rights, seek in this amendment to further that same objective; because they would place the protection in the Interpretation Act, which could be amended much more readily and with much less public interest and discussion than an amendment to the bill of rights. Indeed, I suggest that their amendment would make it possible to change, by implication, the rule of interpretation which they have in their amendment, because it is just another rule of the Interpretation Act and not made sacrosanct as part of the bill of rights itself.
For all these reasons, but mainly because it changes nothing in effect with respect to the process the courts would have to go through, I a-m opposed to the amendment. It changes nothing with respect to the processes the courts would have to go through, but it does have a very definite and disadvantageous effect in that it seeks to remove from the bill of rights one of the fundamental protections of the Canadian citizen about which this government are concerned, and we are not prepared to see done by

Under the Fisheries Act, for instance, inspectors have the right to seize boats and equipment, anything they think may have been used in contravention of the law. The individual concerned is not even given the protection of a warning that anything he may say may be used in evidence against him. There have been many cases where boats have been seized and held for some time and then returned, but there is no recourse for the individual concerned because this is the law.
In the case of the Feeds Act there is the right to search without a warrant. Protection against self-incrimination and against forced confessions is removed, and excessive fines are provided which constitute cruel and inhuman punishment.

We have had legal advice from the people who are administering this particular legislation. I should like to refer to some of the sections that we would like to see strengthened. The Prime Minister is a very

capable lawyer, with a long history in law, and he must recognize that these are facts. In Canada we have given protection to animals, and we have given the officials concerned with animals more power than we have given to those officials who are dealing with human beings.
The bill of rights gives security in the enjoyment of property and the right not to be deprived thereof except by due process of law. However, section 7 (1) (a) of the Feeds Act empowers a government inspector, who may be any person designated by the Minister of Agriculture-this includes political appointees, Mr. Chairman, if the government wants to make appointments for political reasons-to enter private property, search the premises and any private documents and papers therein, and take away samples, all without the process of a search warrant. This power is contrary to clause 2 (a) of the proposed Canadian bill of rights.
Then there is the fact that self-crimination protection has been removed. Sections 7 (1) (b) and 7 (3) of the Feeds Act require a person to give to a government inspector documentary and oral information upon which a criminal charge may be laid against that person. Clause 3 (d) of the proposed bill of rights provides that no act of parliament shall authorize an authority to compel a person to give evidence if that person is denied protection against self-crimination.
Then, too, protection against a coerced confession has been removed. By these subsections parliament abrogates the human right of freedom that a person shall not be coerced to confess. This is so because section 9 makes it an offence for a person to refuse to give written or oral information, or for the person to make a false or misleading written or oral statement, to a government inspector. The penalty for refusing such information or for making a false or misleading statement ranges on summary conviction from a fine of up to $500 to a fine of up to $500 plus up to six months in jail, and upon indictment to a maximum of $2,000 plus one year in jail. In both cases, in addition, there may be confiscation of whatever property the government inspector reasonably believes was used in committing or in relation to committing the offence. Under the threat of such punishment, this parliament has decreed this session that coerced confessions are legal under the Feeds Act. The proposed bill of rights is at variance with this decree in providing in clause 3 (d) that no act of parliament shall deprive a person of a constitutional safeguard against self-crimination.

Now, Mr. Chairman, this cruel and inhuman punishment clause also applies to excessive fines. I may say that earlier this session I raised a point of order when the Prime Minister introduced this bill, not in a facetious way but in a serious manner, because I believed we had already passed a bill this session which would eliminate many of these rights which we propose to give under this bill. However, that matter never came to a decision, and I am not raising it now. We did do some work on this Feeds Act, and it is not by any means the worst of the statutes we have on the statute books in Canada. If the Prime Minister would like to make a detailed examination he can check them himself and he will probably come to a similar conclusion.
I should like to refer to the provisions dealing with arbitrary detention and liberty of the person. Under section 7 (1) (b) and 7 (3) of the Feeds Act an inspector is also empowered to deprive a person of his right not to be arbitrarily detained. Any and every person in the premises must remain at the behest of the inspector and, surrendering the liberty of his person, assist the inspector either by giving information or by physical assistance, as the inspector may require. Well, of course, this would be in contravention of the rights given to the individual under the bill of rights.
I think this amendment which has been suggested is a good amendment, because it would seem to me that the minister would have to give consideration to new legislation that may come before parliament. I would hope, in addition, that the provision would cover government legislation as well as private bills. It appears to me that the clause means that the Minister of Justice is going to look at all new legislation in the light of the provisions contained in the bill of rights. It seems to me that he is going to have to look at the legislation that has been passed already, as well.
It shocked me to hear the Minister of Justice stand up and say that he thinks the courts are going to be able to make decisions because we will have passed this bill of rights. If, for example, a fisherman out on the west coast had a boat loaded with fish and the inspector came aboard to say he was detaining this boat; then a week later,
Human Rights
when the fish were all rotten, he said he had not found anything wrong and therefore the fisherman was free to do whatever he liked with the fish, this would be a contravention of the fisherman's rights. However, if the fisherman has to go before a court to say that this action has contravened his rights as guaranteed by the Canadian bill of rights, if he is going to have to fight the case on that basis then my understanding of the purpose of the bill of rights is all wrong.
I feel the Canadian people have the right to assume that they have certain fundamental rights extended to them by this bill, and that no act of parliament is going to take away those rights. Unless we start from that basis, that people have these fundamental rights and that all legislation should be brought into line with our thinking today in so far as a bill of rights is concerned, then we are being very silly. If a man has to go to court and base his case on what is in the bill of rights, then that it not what I have understood the Prime Minister to say this bill of rights means.
The Prime Minister has said that we have certain expressed freedoms, we have certain expressed rights, and that those rights should be a basic part of all legislation in Canada. I am not saying that we should go back more than 20 years to ascertain whether or not these rights are protected in the various legislative measures passed in Canada. Many times a smart lawyer will look back many, many years to find a precedent or a procedure that has not been heard of for a long time, and will use it as a defence. I am not suggesting that we should go back that far to change these laws. However, I do believe we should change those laws that we know are in conflict with the bill of rights.
The immigration laws, Mr. Chairman, are a good example. In some cases we grill people without even giving them the right to counsel. We make deals. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has made deals which she has no right to make. She has made these offers to citizens who are outside the law, and which do not allow for due process of law, as the bill of rights says. I have right now, for instance, a case where a citizen of this country for 47 years applies for a passport and has no right whatsoever to go before any court; he has no right, under any existing legislation, to go before the court and be given a reason why he has not been given a passport. The reason, Mr. Chairman, is very simple. This particular gentleman has supported the communist party for a number of years and has gone to a number of communist front organizations. But this organization is not illegal; it is permissible to belong

Human Rights
to it, and this gentleman has a fundamental right to belong to that particular political faith if he so wishes. If the Canadian parliament wishes to outlaw it, then I think this would be a reason. But I do not think it should be prohibited by any officials of the department, who can say, "Sure, you can leave Canada; but we will give you no assurance that you can return, although this has been your home for 47 years and you have done nothing illegal".
These are fundamental rights that should be written into our laws, and they should be changes in the existing legislation and regulations. We should do this without an individual having to go to court with all the expense of fighting these cases on his own. If we are not, as a legislative body, willing to go back and examine the legislation we have on the statute books now, while we are dealing with a bill of rights, then I think we are not really saying that we want a bill of rights. What we seem to want is a bill of rights on paper, but we want to have all the abuses that have been inherent in much of our legislation over the years.
We have another case right now before parliament. It is a case to which the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister should give some consideration in this respect. One of the special committees is meeting right now discussing whether we have the power, when we ask for an investigation into a situation, to require those people to appear here. Mr. Chairman, in my humble opinion, if this bill of rights is to mean anything, if it is to be at all effective as I am sure the Prime Minister would like it to be, the Minister of Justice should give very serious consideration to the amendment that has been proposed. I am rather surprised to find that there seems to be a contest going on here with the Minister of Justice as to his knowledge of law and the knowledge of law of other people. I have great respect for the knowledge of the Minister of Justice on the law, and he may well be right; but I do not think a serious amendment such as the one now before us should be so lightly and off the cuff discarded and a series of reasons given for it.
I am sure it could have had the very serious contemplation that was given to it by eminent counsel in Canada, by the Canadian Bar Association and by many notable lawyers. I do not want to think the Minister of Justice considers himself the oracle or the repository of all legal opinion; that he is infallible in
AUGUST 3/ I960
interpreting the amendment or in interpreting the law. Surely that is not quite right. Notwithstanding his rather lengthy, detailed and complicated explanation of why he does not accept the amendment, I am not at all sure that I am impressed.
To quote an illustration, under this bill of rights-I feel sure that the Prime Minister will agree with me on this-in clause 2, paragraph (e), no law of Canada shall be construed or applied so as to:
... deprive a person of the right to a fair hearing in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice ...
We have, for example, the Immigration Act, section 39, which denies the right of appeal. I only give this to the minister as an illustration. What will be given precedence? Will it be the Immigration Act, when the matter comes before a court, or will it be the bill of rights? The Immigration Act says you have no right of appeal; the bill of rights says you shall not be deprived of the right to a fair hearing in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice.
There are other acts on the statute books which contain sections that say the interpretation of the section shall always be in favour of the government. That could be so, even for those in conflict with the bill of rights. This is a series of such statutes on our statute books, and it is my respectful submission that where there is any doubt as to the proper application of the bill of rights the benefit of the doubt should be given to the people of Canada, not to the interpretation which the Minister of Justice almost unilaterally seems to be giving to it.
I think the amendment which the hon. member for Essex East has presented is the crux of the entire effectiveness of this bill of rights. It safeguards the people of Canada against all the statutes which contain provisions which seem to impinge upon the rights of the individual, which the bill of rights wants to restore. I have great respect for the gentlemen sitting in front of the Minister of Justice. I wonder if they have made a study of this matter. I wonder, if they had had before them this amendment that is now before us, whether they could have presented logical explanations regarding the objections they have to our interpretation.
I think the minister would do the country, and the legislation, a world of good if he would make it possible, in the case of any doubt, to interpret the use, the effectiveness, the feasibility and the practicability of the bill of rights in favour of the people of Canada, or of the person who feels himself aggrieved. That is the very spirit of the act, and I submit respectfully, along with the hon.
Human Rights
member for Essex East, that the amendment should be adopted. I think this amendment was wisely conceived and carefully planned. The minister will do himself and the Prime Minister a great injustice if he does not accept it.

I do not propose to restate my argument. I have stated it, and the hon. member for Cartier has elaborated on it. This is the crux of the matter. The bill depends on its interpretation, either the one the minister gives to it or the one that we have placed on it. This is the clause of the bill that will give substance to the effectiveness of this measure or which will mean that it will have no teeth, no effectiveness whatsoever.
The amendment I have put forward, as the minister knows, is an amendment which was suggested after close consultation with one of the best constitutional lawyers of this country, a man who has had long and distinguished experience in the Department of Justice. The hon. gentleman knows that Mr. Mundell has a place second to no one in the administration of the affairs of justice in this country. He was the one selected by the Canadian bar as chairman of its civil liberties division. He is now professor of constitutional law at Osgoode Hall. However, the minister has taken his position and he must bear the consequences.
I am not going to answer the hon. gentleman's remarks about the purpose we have in mind in putting forward the amendment. The Minister of Justice has a great capacity for facilitating the passage of measures in which he is interested. He uses that biting, friendly, benevolent, carping criticism that seeks in one breath to mollify and in the next to kill; all in the process, of course, of enabling the passage of legislation.
The hon. gentleman may want to reconsider what he has said. Whether he does or not is of no concern to anyone. Suffice it to say this; that as the Prime Minister said of the committee which examined the bill of rights, all members who were present applied themselves seriously to this matter, and that, I may say, includes the Minister of Justice. So when we put forward an amendment, which does not satisfy the great legal attainments of the Minister of Justice we are, of course, accused of seeking to block the measure merely because we do not agree with the man who happens to be Minister of Justice. I would have thought that the Minister of Justice, acting in that capacity, would recognize that on points of law he should take a lofty, objective position and find it possible to disagree without entering into a kind of

Human Rights
argument which possibly would be justified on some other occasion in connection with some other matter.
But, as I say, we will leave the matter there. We shall see next year who is right; whether the Canadian Bar Association is right, with its great accumulation of legal knowledge, or the hon. gentleman, with the vast store of legal equipment that has suddenly descended on him. I ask the hon. gentleman to consider, too, whether the courts are going to interpret existing inconsistent legislation such as the Railway Act, chapter 293; the Pipe Lines Act, chapter 211, sections 28 and 29; the War Measures Act, chapter 288, section 3; the Compensation (Defence) Act; the Canadian National Railways Act; the Canadian Broadcasting Act; the National Harbours Board Act; the national hospital insurance act; the narcotic and drug control act; the Immigration Act; the Lord's Day Act-I ask the Minister of Justice, the lord chancellor, as it were of our country, whether he thinks the Supreme Court of Canada in the light of the way this bill now stands, when confronted with concrete situations, is going to say that a specific act inconsistent with the generality of this measure is to take second place to this bill.
That is the argument of the hon. gentleman. He has made it, and we have provided our answer. All one can do is await the results which will be represented by what will happen in the courts of this land when lawyers resort to this bill of rights as a means of providing defences in criminal cases, or as a means of providing responses in civil cases, all of which could be avoided if the Minister of Justice would accept responsibility and put in this bill language which would clearly have the effect which this amendment provides.
My final observation is this. The minister himself said he wanted the act, for the purpose of public relations and legitimate propaganda, divided so the preamble and sections 1 and 2 would stand by themselves. If the effect of amending the Interpretation Act is as the hon. gentleman says, that effect would be consistent with the declared objective he had in mind. In any event, I am sure the hon. gentleman's legal advisers will tell him, if he does not know already, that the Interpretation Act is the basic statute by which parliament and the executive seeks to deal with abridgements and amendments in cases, where there is a whole series of amendments which cannot be fully dealt with.
That is the gist of the amendment. The hon. gentleman has not accepted it. He prefers to place his own judgment ahead of that of the Canadian Bar Association.

I rise not so much to refute what the hon. member has just said as to give an additional reason why this amendment should not be accepted.
I am not going to enter into a debate with the hon. gentleman from Essex East as to whose attitude in this committee has been more appropriate. I simply remind the committee that the hon. gentleman himself has a peculiar approach to these matters. He seems to believe that the right to reply should be entirely on one side and that it does not matter what sort of argument or in what terms, larded with what undesirable or offensive innuendo, he speaks, those on this side have no right to put forward a contrary point of view. But I shall leave it there. The committee has heard the discussion and the committee will decide upon which side lies the responsibility for any, shall I say, sharp exchanges which may have taken place.
I admit at once that it is desirable in discussions of this kind to keep them on a high plane at all times. I suppose the obligation in that respect does lie a little more on this side than it does on the hon. gentleman, and there I perhaps pay him an indirect compliment when I say he has a facility for rapidly reducing discussion to levels to which perhaps it is desirable it should not descend.
But let us deal with this question, and I shall be glad to deal with it quite objectively. I do not for a moment question the ability of Mr. Mundell, nor do I say that in the mind of the Minister of Justice personally rests this vast store of knowledge that warrants his rejecting this amendment. I say simply that as a result of the best consideration we can give the question we have concluded that the views put forward by the hon. member for Essex East, whether they be his own or not, in this amendment are not acceptable because they do not serve the purpose we have in mind for the bill of rights as we have prepared it. I am not going to repeat my earlier arguments, but I shall add one further argument which substantiates the position I have taken.
If the committee will read carefully the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Essex East, hon. members will find that although it might be operative with respect to statutes it is almost entirely deficient with respect to regulations, rules and orders, whereas our bill of rights by a combination of clause 2 and the interpretation provision in clause 5 will have effect with respect not only to the statutes but with respect to all orders, rules and regulations made thereunder in the future as well as in the past.

If you look at subsection 1 of the amendment you will find that it reads:
Every act of the parliament of Canada and every order, rule and regulation thereunder in force at the commencement of this section, and all laws in Canada that are subject to be repealed, abolished or altered by the parliament of Canada in force at the commencement of this section, are hereby amended by repealing or revoking them-
Regulations that are in force at this time
would, it is true, be affected by the provision as it is drawn but the amendment is deficient because it does not contain a provision to bring regulations hereafter enacted, under its operation. It is true that subsection 2 does refer to "no act of the parliament of Canada passed hereafter" but that omits all reference to regulations or orders, and "act of parliament of Canada" is not a phrase which is included in the definition of law as we have it in the bill. It is by reason of our definition of "law" our bill has application to all orders and regulations made under statute. There is a vital deficiency in the amendment as drawn.
This, it may be argued, is perhaps a technical objection to the amendment, but it is one of importance because it reveals that there is a wide field of statutory orders and regulations which we believe a bill of rights should cover, both past and future, that are omitted from the amendment as submitted by the hon. member for Essex East. Because we want our bill of rights to be effective in all fields we, for that additional reason, have come to the conclusion that the amendment should not be accepted.
Amendment (Mr. Martin, Essex East) negatived: Yeas, 22; nays, 32.

Mr. Chairman, I regret that I did not have the opportunity of being associated with the Minister of Veterans Affairs in this motion. He will recall that when the Minister of Justice proposed this amendment I agreed at once to second it. I find it difficult to understand why the minister would not give me that honour. However, the Minister of Justice has followed a narrow course in his interpretations throughout the discussion of this bill, and I suppose one would not expect him to deny that honour to one who at least had spoken up first. I think the amendment is a good one.
What I am about to say is not an answer to what the minister said about the purpose of the present discussion in so far members of the Liberal party are concerned. We prefer to look upon that remark more as a lapse on the part of the Minister of Justice in the highly objective attitude he takes in these matters. It is interesting to note that this important question represents very valuable work on the part of the committee. I wish to refer again to the work done by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, who more than anyone else extricated all of us, including the Minister of Justice, from the difficulty that was posed in clause 2 (b) as it now appears before the committee. The original bill provided for wording which read as follows:
- (b) impose or authorize the imposition of torture, or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment:
That was the wording of old clause 3(b). The minister took the position in the committee that he could not change that wording because of the effect of the declaration of human rights. He pointed out, and correctly, that these words "torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment" were incorporated in the declaration of human rights, and that as Canada had joined in that declaration we could not accept something that was less in the bill of rights.
The minister was rather stubborn. He would not give in on that point notwithstanding the representations that were made by members of the Conservative party as well as by Liberal members. It will be recalled that the hon. member for Greenwood who was there, as I say, amicus curiae, joined with us in the concern we all felt over this measure.

Human Rights
The hon. member for York-Scarborough, who happened to turn up that day, was accorded the right as an interested hon. member to put questions and make his observations. When it was pointed out to him that the words as contained in the bill as originally proposed would do the very thing which he sought to do in the motion he brought before this house during the course of this session, namely abolish capital punishment, he was, of course, very gratified.
I suspect it was only the presence and the gratification of the hon. member for York-Scarborough that caused the Minister of Justice, realizing the dilemna into which his false logic had put him, to decide to accept the recommendation made by the hon. member for Vane ouver-Kings way, who said that the minister might resort to the wording of the bill of rights in England of the seventeenth century and take out "torture" and "inhuman" and "degrading" and put in the words "cruel and unusual". The result was that the committee was satisfied with the arrangement. The only possible dissatisfaction would be that of the hon. member for Scarborough, who will find that all his efforts this session are not going to be backed up by the wording which the Minister of Justice in his omniscience has now put into paragraph (b). I think we all recognize the contribution made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway.
I now wish to refer to clause 2 (f) of the bill, where among the most important single rights are those put there as a result of the contribution and recommendation made by the hon. member for Fort William. The hon. member for Fort William is not a lawyer but, like the hon. member for Humber-St. George's, he proved to be a useful member of the committee. It was the hon. member for Fort William who pointed out that the bill left out two very important legal rights, which were referred to in the draft bill of the Ontario bar association and in the declaration on human rights. These two important legal rights are the right to be presumed innocent, placing the onus of proving guilt on those making the charge, and the refusal of reasonable bail without just cause. This is one of the rights declared to be sacrosanct in the declaration on human rights.
Other suggestions were made. Accordingly consideration was given by all members of the committee, including those of this party, to obtain elucidations, particularly in clause 2 (d). I merely mention this to indicate that the changes in this section, as in others, were not all made by the minister; they were changes made as a result of the serious study given to this bill by all members of the committee.
