Mr. Chairman, I was dealing with the editorial which appeared in Le Droit of July 30, 1960, and which deals with the attitude of the attorney general in this case. I should like to quote a portion of it.
(Translation):
The Toronto official claimed, on that occasion, that the witness had no right at all to speak French; he forbade Mrs. X to use the services of an interpreter.
Mr. Roberts made three points in his reply. "I do not blame Mr. Yates for rejecting Mrs. X's request", he said. "Personally," he added deferentially, "I would have allowed that lady to testify in French; however," he added with conviction, "English is the only official language in Ontario".
(Text):
That brings me to the federal aspect of this whole matter. As members of the committee know, the right to the use of the two official languages in so far as parliament is concerned is to be found in section 133 of the British North America Act, which reads as follows:
Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the debates of the houses of the parliament of Canada and of the houses of the legislature of Quebec; and both these languages shall be used in the respective records and journals of those houses; and either of those languages may be used by any person or in any pleading or process in or issuing from any court of Canada established under this act, and in or from all or any of the courts of Quebec.
It is clear that under this section the very same thing which happened in the cases I have mentioned could take place under the federal jurisdiction. If a hearing were held before a board which was not a court of federal jurisdiction, if, for instance, a witness was giving evidence before the board of transport commissioners, although I have some doubt there because it has been declared to be a court of record, or before the air transport board or the many commissions which are not covered by this section of the British North America Act, it might well be that the person presiding might take the same attitude as did the judge in the case in eastern Ontario some years ago to which I have referred and the commissioner under the municipal act who has heard and is still hearing evidence in an adjoining community while we in the parliament of Canada are discussing a bill of rights.
So it would seem to me, Mr. Chairman, here is one case where there being doubt,-in fact, where there being no longer any doubt because the commissioner or the person presiding could do exactly as was done in the

former cases-that doubt should be removed. It would strike me that there should not be the slightest hesitation on the part of those who sit on the other side to grant the privilege-the right, not the privilege-of being heard in their own language, no matter what that may be.
I understood the Minister of Justice to say that that was covered by (e) and (f), but let me say this. Supposing the commissioner, under a federal board, takes the attitude which I am sure the commissioner in the Eastview case must have taken-when he said, I did give a fair trial to that person; in my opinion it was not unfair to refuse the right to an interpreter. Assuming that is done under a federal board, then that is not a right which an individual has. It then becomes a right which the commissioner or chairman has under the circumstances and that is why it seems to me that this is a reasonable amendment. I should add that it is a matter of custom in certain parts of the province of Ontario to allow an interpreter. I know that in many courts and in many areas where I have appeared immediately a witness states that he or she is unable to speak the English language the judge offers the use of an interpreter. However, this is not a right to which the witness is entitled, certainly not under this bill. I am sure that that is not the intention of the Minister of Justice, knowing him as I do.
It seems from what the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont said a moment ago that there was some hesitation about this amendment at one time. Perhaps I am wrong about that, and the Minister of Justice will say whether or not that is the case. I have a feeling that there was some hesitation, and if that be so there is every reason why there should have been, particularly in the light of section 133 of the British North America Act and particularly in the light of the repetition of events which has taken place elsewhere, taking place before a board or tribunal under federal jurisdiction. I am sure the Prime Minister would not want that to happen. I am sure that is not the intention of the bill of rights. If it is not put in specifically I do not think it is enough to say that he shall have a fair trial because here it was thought in the hearing in Eastview that a fair trial was being given to this individual, but none the less there was no right granted to the witness to have the evidence given in the language of her choice.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: That was not a trial.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
The Prime Minister is quite right; that was not a trial, it was an inquiry within the purview of the municipal act. There might be similar inquiries under federal jurisdiction. I thought of the air

transport board as I went along earlier. There are many, many boards under federal jurisdiction. I could get my directory, and I am sure I could list 30 or 40 of them, if not more, where circumstances such as these could repeat themselves.
I hope that those who sit on the other side of the house will accept what I have said in the sentiment in which it is put forward. It is put forward because I believe that here a right was taken away. This bill, in its clause 2 and all the other particulars that are mentioned therein, will not cover a repetition of a situation such as this under federal jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Laurier is quite correct in his interpretation of what took place in the committee. There was some hesitation in respect to this amendment which was offered there, for the very considerations put forward when the hon. member made the appeal he just made. This is a matter which is obviously one where there would be the greatest hesitation, not only to turn down but even to appear to turn down a suggestion that on its face mentions the right to an interpreter on the part of a person who cannot understand the proceedings before the court.
The point I made in the committee, and on the basis of which I asked for time for consideration, was that in my view the right to an interpreter is covered under subparagraphs (e) and (f) of this clause. I said in the committee, and I am reading from page 693 of the evidence:
I have no hesitation in saying that to refuse to grant a person the services of an interpreter, if he is unable to understand the language being used in the procedures of the court, is not a fair hearing: I would say it was a grossly unfair hearing, and I make that statement of fact or principle without saying that it is applicable to the case that you have cited-
That was the Eastview case.
-because I do not know the facts of that case.
I did make the statement of principle that to refuse to allow a person the services of an interpreter if he does not understand the language being used in the proceedings in the court constitutes an unfair hearing. It was because I held that view so strongly that I could not contemplate any reviewing court before which it was established that a person in a court or tribunal below who could not understand the language being used was, nevertheless, refused the services of an interpreter, which would not come immediately to the conclusion it was an unfair hearing, and therefore the bill of rights would apply. They would say this man has been deprived of his right to a fair hearing, and therefore would we find the proceedings below are a nullity. In my opinion that would
Human Rights
follow automatically. It was for that reason that I asked for time to consider, to reassure myself or to consider further the question of whether clauses (e) and (f) were a sufficient answer to the request for an amendment.
At that time I came to the conclusion both that it was covered by the clauses and that it was a sufficient answer to the amendment. On reflection, however, I think I should say that while I am still of the view it is covered in the bill as provided, and I am still strongly of that view, I think there is a question about whether that view is a sufficient answer to the suggestion that it might be incorporated in a bill of rights.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS

I have, therefore, been impressed with the point of view which suggests that since some magistrates or tribunals in the first instance may say, "I am giving a fair hearing", and the person before them will not be able to rely upon the bill of rights as to exactly what a fair hearing is, they may be denied a fair hearing in the first instance and thus compelled to resort to some sort of appeal procedure. Because this point is so important I have been impressed, and I do not mind admitting that it may be second thought, with the argument that we should avoid the possibility that the person concerned may be put to the necessity of appeal; that we should put it in the bill of rights and make it clear to all courts and all tribunals under our authority-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
We will not go into that at the moment. We did pause to consider this matter when it was brought up in the standing committee, and I would still want to pause and consider the terms of the amendment offered here, because I would find some difficulty in accepting it in the terms in which it is offered. I do so for the reason that it does not now, nor did it in the special committee, contain anything which ties the right to the services of the interpreter to a person who is in anyway before the court. It simply says:
Deprive a person of the right to have the free assistance of an interpreter if he cannot understand or speak the language used in court, or before a board or tribunal.
I recognize this is carrying the argument rather far; but, as I see it, on the basis of that wording a spectator might put forward the argument-and there are eccentrics in the country-and say, "Your bill of rights says a person shall not be deprived of the right to an interpreter if he cannot understand the language used in court; I am here, I cannot understand the language; I demand the right to an interpreter". I know that is not the intention; but I think that in drawing up provisions of the bill of rights we must make sure they do not carry it further than the point to which we want to go; and the point to which we want to go, surely, is to ensure that a person whose rights are in question, whose rights or obligations are in question before the court, shall have it established that he has the right to an interpreter if he does not understand the language being used in the court. To that point we are quite prepared to go, as a result of the reconsideration along the lines that I have outlined here.
There is perhaps a further question with respect to the word "free". I do not want to express any firm opinion on this at the moment. However, the use of the word raises questions as to the obligation to pay for the interpreter, and that would be a matter that would be extremely difficult to embrace within the provisions of this kind of bill. It is my own view that if you establish the right to have an interpreter the court will see to it, without any difficulty, that those services are made available if there should be any question of payment. That is another reason why I find it difficult to accept the amendment as drafted.
We have an amendment here which we have been considering and which I should like to read to the committee. Perhaps there will then be further discussion of the matter and in the course of that discussion there could be further consideration given as to the wording to be ultimately adopted. The amend-

ment here is that there should be added a paragraph, known as (g) as follows:
(g) deprive a person of the right to the assistance of an interpreter in any proceedings for the determination of his rights or obligations before a court, commission, board or other tribunal, if he does not understand or speak the language in which such proceedings are conducted.
This, Mr. Chairman, does contain some of the words of the expression that I used before the special committee which I read from page 693, when I said:
I have no hesitation in saying that to refuse to grant a person the services of an interpreter, if he is unable to understand the language being used in the procedures of the court, is not a fair hearing;-
You will see that is largely incorporated into the last words of this suggested amendment "if he does not understand or speak the language in which such proceedings are conducted". So because we are intensely concerned to provide a fair hearing for all those who come to our country, who live in our country, who are entitled to the protection of our laws, whatever may be the language they speak, we are prepared, on the further consideration for which I asked in the special committee, to accept the suggestion that this is one particular that should be written into the bill of rights over and above the provisions that we have already written into it.
I would be happy at the appropriate moment to suggest the moving of this amendment, or something close to it; but I am afraid I could not accept the amendment presented by the hon. member for Maison-neuve-Rosemont in the form in which it is actually drawn.

In fact, I think the minister went on and said that in his opinion it would be a grossly unfair hearing. I was very happy to hear him say that and to know that it is on the record.
But what prompts me to rise again is that even though the Minister of Justice feels strongly about the matter, as he does, and

as strongly as those of us who have advanced the amendment, none the less, as he knows, this would have no bearing whatever upon a commissioner or upon a chairman of a board. The Minister of Justice could be a man with tremendous tolerance, but none the less the chairman of a board could feel otherwise. In fact, that is exactly what happened in the Eastview case. Here the Minister of Justice thinks that this would not be a fair trial, I am sure, having regard to his statement, that he was not aware of the facts.
But there is no doubt, on the other hand, that the individual, the commissioner in this case, was of the view that he was giving a fair trial to this person. I do not think I should pursue the matter any further. The point has been made that the principle of the amendment has been accepted. Whether or not the wording is satisfactory, I am not in a position to say. I hope it will be. I have not seen it and I do not know whether it has been drafted and sent over to us yet, but I would like very much the opportunity of looking at it. However, it is certainly a step in the right direction and I am sure all of us who have been pressing so hard, particularly the hon. member for Essex East and the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rose-mont, will feel satisfied that progress has been made in this direction.

While I am on my feet I should like to make a comment about the procedure in the committee at that time. We all went into that committee with open minds and with only one object in view, namely to make the bill as effective as possible. The
minister and the chairman always gave consideration to the amendments which were put forward and when it was felt they could be incorporated in the bill the necessary action was taken.

I should like to make some remarks pursuant to what was said by the hon. member for Laurier. The attorney general of Ontario, Mr. Kelso Roberts, made a statement which I should like to challenge and condemn when he said that the French language is not official in Ontario. The Quebec act of 1774 could very well have been called the Canada act of 1774 because the limits of the province of Quebec as referred to in that act included Quebec as it is now, Labrador and Ontario as we know it today. The British North America Act did not diminish any of the rights concerning the use of the French language existing under the Quebec act when it was passed in 1867, so I maintain that the French language is official not only in Quebec but in Ontario.
I think it was a very poor show that the attorney general of Ontario should have condoned to a certain degree the decision of Commissioner Yates not to allow a witness to give her evidence in her own language. I think it was a poor show in the first place to have appointed a commissioner who could not understand French to go to the municipality of Eastview without French speaking personnel.

I wonder if I can bring further to the attention of the committee the amendment suggested by the Minister of Justice which reads as follows:
(g) Deprive a person of the right to the assistance of an interpreter in any proceedings for the determination of his rights or obligations before a court, commission, board or other tribunal if he does not understand or speak the language in which such proceedings are conducted.
What I should like to say to the minister is that the amendment he has submitted would not meet the three cases I have brought forward unless certain words are taken out. Unless the words "for the determination of his rights or obligations" are taken out it would not apply to witnesses. If those words were taken out, and I suggest they should be, the amendment would then, I think, meet the three cases I have put on record in Hansard. Without those words, the amendment would read:
Deprive a person of the right to the assistance of an interpreter in any proceedings before a court.

commission, board or other tribunal if he does not understand or speak the language in which the proceedings are conducted.

We did have in mind the position of witnesses, and considered they would be covered. The provision reads:
Deprive a person of the right to the assistance of an interpreter in any proceedings for the determination of his rights and obligations-
Supposing the party defending, or being investigated calls a witness. The witness would then be giving evidence with respect to the proceedings which were being held for the determination of the rights or the obligations of that party and if in the course of giving that evidence in the interest of the party involved the witness required an interpreter it is my tentative opinion, at any rate, that it would be covered because it could be said that the party required the assistance of an interpreter in order that the witness on whose evidence he was relying might give his evidence in a manner understandable to the court.
I appreciate it might be said that this was drawing things rather fine, but we have done it this way to confine it to a person who is really interested in the proceedings in the court and not someone who is not really involved in any way. It does seem to me that this is covered already, but we can consider it further.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
I think that suggestion is a proper one. This principle has prevailed for many years so far as the courts are concerned. The denial of any person, an accused or a witness, of his right to an interpreter in a court of law is a substantial denial of fundamental justice and as such gives grounds for an appeal.
This goes back to 1916 when in the court of criminal appeal in England a Chinese by the name Lee Kun had been refused or denied the use of an interpreter. He did not understand the English language in which the case was being held. He was convicted and the conviction was squashed. There was no new trial granted because, as hon. gentlemen know, no provision existed at that time in the United Kingdom for a new trial on appeal.
I have seen a number of examples similar to those outlined by the hon. member for Laurier. I think of one case in particular in which the judicial officer refused to consider in any way the right of the individual to speak any language other than the English language. The witness was quite unable to do so. The judicial officer who will also remain unidentified proceeded to excoriate this man for his failure to speak the English language. A conviction was registered. I had something to do with the appeal and it did not take very many minutes before a decision favourable to the appellant was given.
However, the rules in effect as to fundamental justice in this connection do not apply to commissions or boards. In the event that a person is denied an interpreter in a lower court an application by way of prohibition might be launched to assure that the magistrate should not proceed with the case until the opportunity for the witness or accused to have an interpreter was assured. That does not, of course, apply in the case of boards or commissions. There is nothing to guide the chairman or other officials of a board or executive tribunal in assuring the maintenance of fundamental justice.
We have had that in a number of cases. We had that in the Eldorado investigation some years ago in which provision was made by order in council to allow the commissioner to act as he would regardless of whether or not he was within the law. Whatever the

action he took, whether constitutional safeguards were maintained or denied, there was no right of appeal against the action or conduct of that commissioner.
That is the reason why through discussion we bring about in the best traditions of the House of Commons the changes that are necessary. I must say to the hon. member who brought forward this amendment that as soon as I heard it I could not but conclude that it was reasonable, proper and necessary. Even though in so far as cases in court are concerned I feel it would be covered by subclauses (e) and (f); in so far as a commission or executive tribunal is concerned it would not be covered.
I must say that is the essence of parliament in proper operation. It gives me an opportunity to say once more that the special committee that studied this matter was of that nature where, through discussion and consideration, determinations are arrived at for the best interests of all. All that remains now is that we arrive at some amendment that will be generally accepted to meet the consensus of opinion.	[DOT]

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, yesterday
during the general discussion of the bill I gave the reason why a clause should be included which would authorize the establishment of a parliamentary committee similar to the committee which exists in New Zealand, the success of which, I might add, suggests that a similar procedure might work in any parliament for the benefit of the rights and privileges of individual citizens. In this contention I am supported by the submission made by the Seventh Day Adventists, which was read by the Rev. Darren L. Michael, who said:
To sum up the views of the Seventh Day Adventist Church in Canada which warmly applauds the Prime Minister for taking the initiative in introducing such a measure the following points are emphasized with respect to Bill C-79, "an act for the recognition and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms" which it is felt would greatly strengthen the effectiveness of this bill:
I am not going to read all of the recommendations, but I will read recommendation No. 6:
6.	A standing parliamentary committee be established to give continuing examination with reference to the operation of this proposed act in the light of changing circumstances, and
7.	This committee could draft, and parliament accept, a preamble to the bill-
Which was, of course, accepted. I am also supported very warmly in this amendment by no other than the Prime Minister himself. I refer to a statement made by the Prime Minister in 1945, as reported in Hansard at page 2460. Among other things he said:
In the United Kingdom it has been found necessary to set up a committee in this regard,-
I might say it was a question regarding the establishment of the national emergency bill. I continue:
-and I should like to see a similar committee appointed by this house.
Such a committee would report to the house from time to time on all orders in council passed where there is a matter of principle in issue and where the question of delegated power arises. Where legislative power is conferred, the committee would make the necessary criticisms of

orders passed by civil servants under the powers granted by legislation enacted by parliament.
Members of the house would be given an opportunity to serve. There should be no difficulty about the government having a majority in the committee. Its members would be charged with noting any breaches of parliamentary privileges and democratic rights; in fact, in orders in council it would be a watchdog in the preservation of our democratic rights.
That was in 1945. In 1951 the Prime Minister had this to say in speaking about the proposition to establish a committee on civil rights:
My suggestion, sir, is that in view of the importance of civil liberties and their preservation, there be set up a standing committee of the House of Commons on civil rights ...
This committee would correlate information regarding interference with civil liberties as they take place. It would give publicity thereto. It would make Canadians everywhere cognizant and constantly aware of invasions of our basic liberties and of the inadequacy in many cases of our present laws in guarding those liberties. It would make Canadians freedom conscious, for this committee would provide parliament with a watching brief over freedom regardless of what may be the distribution of powers under the British North America Act.
I do not intend to go on much longer, Mr. Chairman, because the proposal has been discussed at length during the general discussion of the bill of rights and also extensively discussed in the special committee. I feel confident that the Prime Minister must have a sympathetic outlook toward this proposal. I am offering this amendment in the hope that the Prime Minister will accept it unless he has changed his mind since 1951. I am quite satisfied he will do what I think is the correct thing to do and accept this amendment. I think a committee such as is contemplated in the amendment will be able to make a substantial contribution to the bill of rights. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's:
That clause 3 be amended by adding thereto:
(a)	Reports of inconsistency from the Minister of Justice shall be referred to an appropriate standing committee of the House of Commons on human rights and fundamental freedoms.
(b)	All petitions to the House of Commons which purport to be based on the Canadian bill of rights shall be referred to an appropriate standing committee of the House of Commons on human rights and fundamental freedoms. The committee shall have power to report these petitions from time to time to the house, together with its opinions and observations thereon.
All I can say is that the adoption of this amendment would greatly strengthen the bill of rights.

Mr. Chairman, I recollect very well the circumstances under which on a number of occasions I suggested in the house that a standing committee of the House of Commons should be set up to act, as the hon. member said, as a watchdog in order 79951-0-473J
Human Rights
to guard against encroachments on and invasions of freedoms within the jurisdiction of parliament. I believe this is an objective which will be attained in due course provided the House of Commons, which is the master of its own rules, will bring about the setting up of such a committee. Through the years I have advocated that and I am unchanged in my viewpoint that we should all become freedom conscious, that the tendency and trend toward passing orders in council with almost prodigal disregard of human freedoms should end, and to that end that a standing committee of the house should be set up.
I still believe that parliament should give consideration to that matter. The means of bringing about a change in the rules is, of course, provided for under the traditions of parliament. I do not, however, believe that the setting up of such a committee should be incorporated in a bill of rights as such. I agree with the hon. member that it would be most desirable to bring about the setting up of such a standing committee. At the next session of the house I hope that the committee on rules, which has been in existence during the present session, will be constituted at the earliest possible date and that when it is constituted the direction of the thinking of that committee will in one respect, among others, be toward reaching a recommendation to the House of Commons for a standing committee along the lines indicated by the hon. member. That is a course that I believe to be very beneficial.
There was a time when orders in council did not find their way before the House of Commons. Indeed, as I recall, there was one order in council passed in September of 1945, the existence of which was denied in November, 1945, although I knew it existed from information I had received. Finally, in February, 1946, Mr. King, the then prime minister, announced that the particular order in council had been forgotten by the minister of justice. That was the order in council that swept aside habeas corpus, that denied to the individual the right to those constitutional safeguards which we are now incorporating in the bill of rights and the preservation of which I hope will be assured under the bill of rights now before the house.
While the House of Commons must always be the master of the course which it will follow, I think it would be the desire of all members of the house that when the committee on rules is set up at the next session it should give the fullest consideration to this matter, and I hope that hon. gentlemen will approve the setting up of such a committee as is suggested in the amendment in

Human Rights
order to ensure that there shall be no derogation from, no diminution of, the freedoms which we are now setting forth as declaratory of our purposes and aims under a bill of rights.

Mr. Chairman, the amendment moved by the hon. member for Fort William is one that was introduced by him with respect to former clause 2 of the bill as presented on second reading. I think the hon. member is to be congratulated on the initiative he has shown in the formulation of this proposal.
To fully understand its worth, I think one must have an appreciation of what took place in connection with clause 3 now before us. The original clause in the bill was certainly not in this form, and the suggestions and improvements made were as a result of the suggestions offered by members of this party in that committee. The committee will recall that when the clause was presented on second reading the Leader of the Opposition objected to a change in the wording of the bill, as contained in the present draft in comparison with the bill put forward in 1959. At that time the clause read that the Minister of Justice shall, in accordance with such regulations as may be prescribed by the governor in council, examine every proposed regulation submitted in draft form to the clerk of the privy council and every bill introduced in the House of Commons in order to ensure whether any of the provisions thereof are inconsistent with the purposes and provisions of this part.
That was the way the bill stood in 1959. When the bill came before us this year on second reading instead of the word "ensure" there was the word "ascertain", which placed a higher obligation on the actions of the minister than is contained at present and as was contained in the bill when presented on second reading. The Leader of the Opposition thought that the clause lacked sanction, that the clause had no teeth, that it did not impose any duty on the Minister of Justice that was not then present.
Surely the Minister of Justice, he argued, would be expected to examine all draft regulations, and indeed all regulations and all government bills to see whether they conformed in terms with the bill of rights or whether they were inconsistent. There were no additional functions imposed on the Minister of Justice, the Leader of the Opposition argued. When the bill went to the committee, I think I must say that there was a general disposition on the part of all members to recognize that the clause needed something, that the clause meant nothing as

it stood. All members of the committee did not support the amendment of the hon. member for Fort William. As a matter of fact, the amendment was defeated on a division as between parties represented in the committee, that is excluding the representative of the C.C.F. who was not present.
Now, the minister, after being pressed by the members of the committee, once the resolution of the hon. member for Fort William had been disposed of, came back to the committee with the addition of the words that are now in the clause, that he shall report any such inconsistencies to the House of Commons at the first convenient opportunity. Speaking on behalf of our party in that committee I said that was a welcome advance made by the minister. However, it did not meet the full views of the members of the Liberal party. It represented a disposition on the part of the minister, at long last, to recognize that there were views outside of the ministry of justice that deserved attention. It was an encouraging display of flexibility which, up until that time, had not been forthcoming.
The minister had made an advance. We agreed that all draft regulations should not come before the house because those were matters as between members of the cabinet. In so far as any government bill was concerned, there would be no doubt and there is an obligation, by implication, on the minister to report any inconsistencies in so far as the bill of rights is concerned with regard to any bill which may be introduced in this house.
We also were inclined to suggest to the minister that it was not satisfactory to say he should report any such inconsistencies to the House of Commons at the first convenient opportunity. I believe I raised the question that the words "at the first convenient opportunity" were not sufficient and should we not say so many days after the opening of parliament the minister should make a report. I must say, in fairness to the minister, that he satisfied me that in the first year we ought to see, by trial and error, what the situation might be. It was agreed, therefore, that we would leave the clause in its present form on that understanding. We will be interested in knowing next session, if there is going to be a next session of this parliament, if the minister has been able to examine all the inconsistencies in existing legislation and report the same to the house, together with inconsistent regulations.
The amendment of the hon. member for Fort William, I think, should be accepted now. The Prime Minister spoke in the

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the process of reformation knows no limits. It is really wonderful to sit here and behold the degree of change in the thinldng of the hon. gentlemen opposite.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Since that date no statute has passed parliament or no order in council has been passed by the executive council which in any way has abrogated, interfered with, diminished or reduced the fundamental rights of individuals. That is one of the steps forward that has taken place; one of the things that we promised we would bring about, and have brought about.
That does not mean that occasions may not arise when as a result of action taken there might be some interference with fundamental freedoms, some application coming before parliament. The Minister of Justice is charged to examine all applications that come before parliament and to:
-examine every proposed regulation submitted in draft form to the clerk of the privy council pursuant to the Regulations Act and every bill introduced in or presented to the House of Commons. in order to ascertain whether any of the provisions thereof are inconsistent with the purposes and provisions of this part and he shall report any such inconsistency to the House of Commons at the first convenient opportunity.

It could not be clearer than that. If in consequence of a report, if even in anticipation that that possibility may arise at any time in the future, I believe consideration could be given by the house to the setting up of a standing committee along the lines that I have advocated through the years and now is accepted and adopted by the hon. member for Fort William and those associated with him.
I have already given the assurance that if at the next session of parliament there is any desire on the part of the rules committee-and I hope there will be; and I hope the hon. member for Fort William is on the rules committee, and that can be assured by a simple application to the whip of the opposition, who will be able to pass that information on to the Leader of the Opposition -if the hon. gentleman is on that committee and makes representations in this connection, I hope all hon. members on that committee will adhere to the suggestion made and that a permanent standing committee will be set up.
After all, we have a standing committee on the library of parliament and on the rest of the house-

speechtext: -and I would think a standing committee on freedoms would be appropriate.

Mr. Chairman, I was pleased that a member of the Liberal party moved the amendment that is before the committee but I want to say that I was even more pleased with the statement that has been made by the Prime Minister. I would think that with the assurance of the Prime Minister that this procedure could be followed, the rules committee could consider this question and, if appropriate, make a recommendation to the house so that this committee could be clothed within the rules of the house. I think that is a good suggestion.
I think the Liberal party is performing a useful function by putting forward all these amendments. However, in the light of their own previous record I think they can appear too rigid in the public mind if they do not readily and quickly accept this assurance from the Prime Minister.
We went further than the Prime Minister. You could not have been here.
I know. You are so far ahead of your past that you hope it will be forgotten.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: You are not ahead at all.

That is the position of the Liberal party, and I congratulate them for it. One thing about the Liberal party is that they are always a liberal party when they are in opposition; but give them a few days in government, when there is work to do, and it is a different matter.
Hear, hear.

However, I just wanted to say that I appreciate the statement that has been made by the Prime Minister. I believe that the rules committee of the house, will take this under advisement and bring in a positive recommendation, and I think we could accept this as the opinion of the house as to the course that should be taken in order to bring about the objectives of the amendment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The hon. member for Assin-iboia has joined us again to demonstrate his well-known flexibility. I regret to say that on this occasion we cannot join him in this flexibility for reasons I hope to indicate. The process of reformation which continues to give the Prime Minister so much amusement is nothing to the process of procrastination of which the Prime Minister is now giving us another glaring illustration, because way back in 1945 the right hon. gentleman said he wanted this done, and now we are giving him the chance to do it. The government has been in office three years during which period, presumably, they still wanted this done. The Prime Minister has just told us that during this period of purity there was no such thing as a violation of human rights and fundamental freedoms and therefore no such procedure as this was required. I could talk at length on that score but I would be out of order because some of these matters are now before the courts.
The Prime Minister has said: we shall do it next session; we shall do it by the rules committee; we shall set up a committee on human rights by the same process as we set up a committee on the restaurant. That is not good enough when we are discussing in this House of Commons the promulgation of Canadian rights and liberties. This bill is the place in which to make provision for this committee. If the Prime Minister feels as strongly now as he has indicated he felt about violations of human rights by orders in council being passed and that sort of thing, then surely this is the time to ensure in so far as legislation can ensure it that if this kind of thing happens again it can be examined by a committee of this house and the necessary action taken. Why should it be a committee set up by a decision of the rules committee along with the restaurant committee and the library committee? The
Human Rights
committee should be established by the bill of rights itself and the committee will be given prestige and sanctity by enshrinement in this bill.
Surely the Prime Minister must realize that not only should this be done now but that it should be done in this particular way to justify in his own mind the importance which he has always attached to this matter since 1945.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
I should like to point out a very good reason why this committee of the House of Commons should not be set out in a statute. Are we going to pass a statute which will require to be passed by the Senate in order to become law, and is the Senate going to participate in the setting up of a commons committee? That is something which I think would be a departure from every constitutional principle that has ever been accepted in this country.
In other words, there is no limit to the changing reformation on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite who are now asking the House of Commons to place in a statute a reference to the setting up of a House of Commons committee which will require the support of the Senate in order to achieve it. I think that in itself is sufficient to answer the arguments of the hon. gentlemen.

The setting up of a committee of this house to act in a watchdog role would undoubtedly help assure the enforcement of this bill of rights. What I want to suggest now is something in a more positive vein; not some action that can be taken after the law has been broken but, rather, a positive step to make certain as far as we can that the law is not abrogated.
I am suggesting that within the Department of Justice there should be established a human rights division. I feel that this legislation which parliament is in the process of passing is important legislation. It has the positive support of the Canadian people, and a human rights division within the Department of Justice could do a great deal in promoting the ideas set forth in this

Human Rights
measure and providing additional means of bringing these rights to the attention of Canadian students and to the attention of the public generally. If it is brought from time to time to the attention of the government that there are infractions of the law or that infractions are about to take place, perhaps officers of this proposed division could do a public relations job of talking to the people who are involved and seeing whether they can get them to amend their ways, and seeing to it that Canadians have the rights which are set forth in this legislation.
Another duty of such a human rights division I suggest would be to assist the minister in the examination of regulations and bills to make certain that none were in conflict with this law. I think a human rights division in the Department of Justice would keep this whole idea of basic human rights and fundamental freedoms alive in the minds of the people of the country so that we will not pass from discussing this bill into a general negative atmosphere when everybody is saying: "Is the law being broken; if so, let us take action." That is important but let us do something positive. Let us have a human rights division to promote human rights and fundamental freedoms and provide an avenue of education for Canadians as to their basic rights and the need for all Canadians to conform not only to the letter of the law but to the spirit of the law. I therefore move:
That clause 3 be amended by adding the letter "a" after the numeral "3" in line one, and by adding thereto the following subparagraph (b):
(b) There shall be established within the Department of Justice a special human rights division for the purpose of:
(i)	assisting the Minister of Justice in his examination of regulations and bills pursuant to paragraph (a) of this clause.
(ii)	initiating studies and procedures with a view to improving the general observance of human rights and fundamental freedoms in Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we are in agreement with the amendment moved by the hon. member. It seems to me that this is a useful and constructive amendment and we will be glad to support it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this matter was raised in the special committee and has been considered by us both then and since. It arises out of a suggestion made in Professor Scott's presentation to the committee, as I see it, and I imagine that is where the hon. member for Assiniboia obtained his inspiration. What I pointed out to the special committee it seems to me applies equally now. That is, what we would be doing here is to attempt to write in part of the detail of the organization of the Department of Justice

in a bill of rights. If you are going to do that you have to do things completely. You have to provide for the appointment of officers, the payment of salaries and all the other things that go with the setting up of a human rights division.
It could be said that it is apparent from the nature of the amendment that it is really only a pious hope and my hon. friends have not got down to the bones of what would be necessary to make it a reality. The amendment would have no practical effect if left in its present form.
May I now point out what is perhaps a more fundamental objection. That is, that this is going to be the responsibility of the Minister of Justice by virtue now of the express provisions of clause 3 of the bill we are now considering. I think it would be premature to attempt now to say in detail how the minister will exercise that responsibility. He is going to have to examine every bill introduced in or presented to the House of Commons.
He is going to have to examine all regulations in draft form, and regulations as defined in the Regulations Act include orders and a great number of instruments.
This is going to be, in.my view, a heavy obligation on the part of the Department of Justice. It might well be that we will require additional personnel to discharge this obligation. I think I should make it clear that in some respects it is only an extension but a very broad one of the duties the department has now. It might therefore require additional personnel for the department and on the other hand we may find we can discharge it with the present personnel in the department.
I therefore think it would be completely premature to write into a statute now a matter which is really only dealing with the method by which the minister with the assistance of his departmental officials will discharge the onus the statute places on him. I think it is premature until we have had some experience in this field in working out the way in which the report to parliament should be made, for instance, and a number of other matters that will be covered by the regulation or regulations contemplated in this clause itself.
If we were required to set up a human rights division now, that, as I say, means special personnel and of course special clerical assistance which would mean setting up a new branch the size and extent of which we would not be in a position to judge and committing us to additional expenditures to operate that branch at a time when we do not know whether that expenditure would be justified.

Furthermore the organization we developed might need to be changed from time to time. It seems to me, therefore, the only reasonable course is to let us develop experience and see what is necessary to discharge this obligation and then when we know that, if it is necessary or desirable we can come to parliament and ask for the necessary changes in the Department of Justice Act, if such changes are required.

Mr. Chairman, we moved this amendment because we think it is a step that should be taken. I do not think the minister's arguments remove the need for such course of action. The minister said this would require special personnel and clerical staff. That is certainly one of the purposes of passing it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: But you have not made any provision for that.

This could be done a little later in the legislation. This is not impossible. If the government wanted to do that it would be easy for it to bring in the necessary amendments to provide by regulation for the carrying out of this step and it would be done. Of course, the reason the minister is opposed to the amendment has nothing to do with draftsmanship. It is merely because the government is not yet prepared to take this step.
The minister said this is only a special way of carrying out the functions of the department and the minister as set forth in clause 3. We think it is much more than that. We think it would in fact be an extension of activity in regard to the support of human rights and fundamental freedoms.
This amendment has two parts. The first is that the human rights division obviously would assist the minister in his examination of regulations and bills pursuant to clause 3 as it now stands. The second part of the amendment is that the human rights division would intitiate studies and procedures with a view to improving the general observance of human rights and fundamental freedoms in Canada. Therefore, what we have in mind is much more than the very necessary but limited scope of clause 3. I think that the passage of such an amendment and the establishment of such a human rights division are necessary to strengthen the whole purpose of this legislation, and that if we have within the Department of Justice a human rights division in the days ahead the provisions of this bill would be more securely established, not only in the law itself but in the practice and in the attitudes of Canadian citizens. I think this kind of step will inevitably have to be taken. Now is the time to take it.

If it will inevitably have to be taken, then it should be taken in the proper way. Bills setting up departments and authorizing staff require resolutions because they impose upon the government the obligation of spending money to carry out the statutory provision which is introduced. We, therefore, could not do a thing like this or commit ourselves to do a thing like this without a resolution. That is why I say it should not be inserted in the bill of rights at this time because it is not the kind of provision that you put in a bill of rights. You do not put in a bill of rights a provision to organize or re-organize the Department of Justice.
In addition, I point out that the Saskatchewan bill of rights, I assume, was passed with the intent that it should be an effective measure for creating consciousness and awareness and the enforcement and protection of human rights in Saskatchewan. There is not a single word in that statute as to the organization of the attorney general's department or setting up any division in that department. I hope my hon. friend is not going to say that the attorney general's department is thus less able to carry out any obligation in Saskatchewan that it should have, or any interest that it should take in the bill of rights. Unless my hon. friend is going to criticize the government of his own province of Saskatchewan, may I suggest that they in this respect followed the proper course of not inserting in the bill of rights those things which should not be there.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has a technical argument. I think the proposition in this amendment is a good one. As far as Saskatchewan is concerned, I think the government of that province is to be congratulated on having initiated a bill of rights as long ago as 1947. It may well be that this kind of provision should be in the law in Saskatchewan. On this I do not pose as an authority in any way at all. It may be that if-

for the C.C.F. party nationally. We are encouraged by the good work done in Saskatchewan. The people of that province would be the first to agree that improvements could be made in Saskatchewan.

Mr. Chairman, on second reading of this bill an hon. member argued that there could be no successful contention made that in clause 2 of the bill as presented for second reading there was any invasion of provincial powers, notwithstanding what was said about the word "Canada" or the words of "enjoyment of property"; also, notwithstanding the very able argument put forward in The Canadian Bar Review by Professor Louis- Phillippe Pigeon

of Laval University, who was concerned about the geographic application of the word "Canada" and the meaning of the word "property" in its unrestricted form as conveying to his mind an invasion of provincial powers.
The Minister of Justice will recall that in the committee there was considerable discussion on this point. The member for Belle-chasse joined with myself and others who spoke in expressing, at any rate, the view that clause 2 as drawn at least was doubtful in its full implications in this particular; that nothing could be lost by taking steps to see that the intent as stated by the Prime Minister was respected with legal effect in the act.
When the Prime Minister introduced the bill he quite properly said that the intention was that we should confine what we do to matters within section 91 of the British North America Act. It was pointed out in response to this observation that the courts will not look at what the Prime Minister says or what any hon. member of the house says because in judicial interpretation it is not open to the courts, for the purpose of ascertaining meaning, to examine what was said in the debates of parliament.
For that reason and others it was suggested, first of all by the hon. member for Belle-chasse, that there should be provision made in old clause 2, now clause 1, for the use of phrases that would indicate that we were only dealing with matters within our competence. However, the suggestion having been made that this might be done in the preamble, it was then agreed by the hon. member for Bellechasse, the Minister of Justice and others, that perhaps that was the place to put it.
Although I am not satisfied with the actual wording in the English text of the preamble, I believe that once we bring the words in the English text in conformity with the meaning clearly and unmistakably provided in the French text that will be ample authority for feeling that we have clearly reserved our position so far as powers are concerned. I would argue that to say in the preamble, "shall reflect the respect of parliament for the limits of its constitutional authority" would clearly safeguard our concern in this matter.
But the Minister of Justice caused me to wonder as to his real intentions when he argued, following presentation of the amendment by the hon. member for Assiniboia, that he could not accept that amendment because it was clearly in violation of provincial rights and it could not be argued that the reference to limitation of powers in the preamble really delimited in any way

any of the functions or any of the declarations sought to be asserted in the present clause 1.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I never said any such thing.

I am just saying that is my impression. The Leader of the Opposition and I recall that the minister did make that statement. He may have intended something else but he certainly used words that are open to that interpretation. Whether or not that is the case, and I am not now blaming the minister or pursuing the point I just made, let us be clear about this. I am satisfied that under the rules of interpretation the courts may look at any word in the operative part of the act and say that it means such and such in the light of what is contained in the preamble. The preamble cannot enact but the use of words in the preamble can explain the meaning of words in the operative sections.
But because I am concerned about the minister's observation, because I do want to see this legislation as effective as possible so there can be no doubt about the matter, leaving the preamble precisely as it now is subject to clarification of words, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Maison-neuve-Rosemont:
That clause 5, section 1, be amended as follows:
That the following words shall be added after the word ''act'' in line 16 "nor to apply beyond the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada."

I have them here, page 7423 of Hansard. I said at that time:
Another objection is that whatever the hon. member for Essex East or others may say about the proposed amendment, it does get us into the field of provincial jurisdiction. Whatever words you may put in the preamble indicating your intention to confine the bill to federal jurisdiction, it is, as I understand it, a law of interpretation that if, notwithstanding an expression of intent in a preamble, you introduce into that part of the bill that has legislative effect a provision which clearly goes beyond the intention expressed in the preamble then it is the section of the bill itself to which effect shall be given and not the words of the preamble.
The meaning of these words is very different from the interpretation which the hon. member gave them a few moments ago.
Not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is, of course, a clear rule of interpretation that the courts in applying statutes must have regard to the effective words of the legislative provision and that you cannot by a mere declaration in a preamble pretend, and have the courts give effect to your pretence, that you have limited the confines and the effect of your legislation if your legislation itself clearly goes beyond the declaration of intention in the preamble. That is why we have been so careful in drafting the bill not to go beyond the field of federal legislative competence. That is why we have resisted so strongly all the efforts of my hon. friends in the Liberal and C.C.F. parties which would in our view have had the effect of taking the bill of rights beyond the field of federal legislative competence.
As I said at the beginning of my remarks on this subject, in the special committee the hon. member for Essex East was satisfied that all we should do was to put words of intent into the preamble and, indeed, he resisted in the committee a suggestion advanced by a member of the Conservative party that such words should in fact be included in clause 5.
I beg your pardon, I did not resist. I suggested I was satisfied with the preamble and I did not resist any such suggestion. I should like to know where I did.

There has been some concern about where the jurisdiction of this bill went, and there was a suggestion in the earlier clauses that if there was need to clarify the matter in any way-and I am not saying that there is but that if that were

to be considered, clause 5 might be a convenient place to put that in, to show that it applied to those things within the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada. If it was felt there was a need to clarify that position, it would seem to be a suitable place to have it inserted.
To which I replied:
I think that is an interesting and valuable suggestion, perhaps taken in conjunction with the suggestion that there might also be a short phrase in the preamble. This would be in the act itself, and it might be a very useful way to make it clear to the courts what the intention of the legislature is.
Then my hon. friend immediately replied:
If it were put in the preamble, that would take care of it.
Of course, and that is my contention now,

-us when we have changed our views. I am glad to find the hon. member for Essex East now shares the views of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway.
Therefore, consistent with my previous position, I am quite prepared to accept the principle of this amendment. However, may I point out to the committee that the amendment, as drawn, is in the negative. It is suggested to me that that is not a desirable principle to incorporate into bills by way of direction to the courts. Indeed, it is my view that the insertion of this negative form amounts almost to an impossible direction to the courts because how can the courts in Canada decide they would construe a statute

extending beyond the legislative competence of Canada. This is directing them to avoid doing something which it would be improper for them to do in any event. In that form, we will be quite prepared to accept the amendment.

I thank the minister for his remarkable display of flexibility and the very generous words in which that flexibility was noted. I leave to him the decision as to who shall have the honour of making the motion.

-I am saying that this bill lays it down in black and white that if the War Measures Act is proclaimed, these rights no longer stand in the way of the enactment of the War Measures Act; and we have not got that statement in the law at the moment. This might, in fact-
This amendment:
-weaken our position under the War Measures Act. Maybe the War Measures Act is at the moment more restricted by the principles of human rights than it will be if paragraph (5) of clause 6 is made law. Frankly, I am frightened of that.
We did not go as far as that; in fact, we did not take that position in regard to this
Human Rights
amendment. We thought, and expressed our thought, that this amendment was an improvement, so far as it went, but that it did not go nearly far enough to deal with threats to rights and liberties in time of war or apprehended war, because we all know that wheq. arms clash laws sometimes cease to protect as they do in normal times.
This matter was discussed before the special committee, not only by Professor Scott but by Professor Lower himself. It is a matter to which he has given a great deal of consideration over the years and about which he has written much. He had this to say, as reported on page 318 of the evidence:
This clause, it seems to me, giving parliament-
And this is the amendment he was talking about:
-the power to resolve that the declaration be revoked, does not mean a thing. It fust does not mean a thing because, of course, the government of the day, under that clause, will do as it likes and parliament will obediently follow it, especially in a time of hysteria such as wartime.
I would think today, when within our own country we are relatively peaceful and there are no particular difficulties coming forward, our civil liberties are not in too much danger. I must say I do not find any great complaint about the way things go on.
Then he said later:
It is not in peacetime that our civil liberties are in any overly great danger: it is in wartime, or other such emergencies.
That, of course, is when we need protection most-as experience has shown. When Professor Cohen was questioned about this matter in his evidence, on page 396 he said this:
May I give you my conclusions in two seconds, Mr. Chairman. Let me draw my balance sheet about this bill.
Then he mentioned some points against the bill. His second point was:
-the inadequate consideration of the role of the War Measures Act.
Mr. Mundell, on page 505, took the same position generally when he said this in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Essex East:
Mr. Mundell, have you any comment to make on clause 6 of the bill?
