The present War Measures Act comes into force on a proclamation of the governor in council- which is the government, really-and stays in force until a further proclamation is issued. Parliament could at any time, of course, pass a statute repealing the War Measures Act and declaring it to be of no force and effect.
This provision-
That is the amendment we are discussing:
-permits parliament-the two houses acting together-to pass legislation making the War Measures Act ineffective. To that extent it is an expectation and aids parliamentary control. The likelihood of its being used is, I think, slight.

Human Rights
That is why, I say that while we think this particular amendment has some value when it states:
Sections 3, 4 and 5-
Of the War Measures Act:
-shall come into force only upon the issue of a proclamation of the governor in council declaring that war, invasion or insurrection, real or apprehended, exists.
Then it says:
-shall be laid before parliament forthwith after its issue, or, if parliament is then not sitting, within the first fifteen days next thereafter that parliament is sitting.
Then parliament can, in its wisdom, take action in respect of the proclamation. I think, as I have said, that that is an improvement but, according to so many of the witnesses who testified before the special committee, it is not an improvement that is going to be as effective under war conditions in protecting human rights and liberties as they thought desirable.
The Prime Minister has always had a great interest in this matter, and far back in 1947 he advocated far more drastic action in respect of the War Measures Act than that which is included in this amendment. I am quoting the Prime Minister from a debate with which the committee will be quite familiar, because it has been referred to so many times in this discussion. It is the debate of May 16, 1947, and on page 3157 of Hansard the present Prime Minister is reported as saying:
I have a few suggestions to make. The first one is that this committee should consider the advisability of the repeal of the War Measures Act which has been on the statute books since 1914.
Then he said:
It was passed by the Sir Robert Borden government in 1914.
Mr. Ian Mackenzie said, when he intervened:
A very necessary act, too.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
My right hon. friend says it was a very necessary act. It was necessary in the period of the war; but in the days of peace, with the challenge that the state is making to the rights of the individual. Professor Lower supports the stand that I take, namely, that the act should be repealed.
We on this side of the chamber do not go so far as the Prime Minister went at that time. But we do think that this amendment should be strengthened and made more effective for the purpose which we all have in mind. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin):
That subsection (5) of section 6 be deleted and that there be added the following section as section 6A:

"6A (1) Subject to subsection 2, any act or thing done or authorized or any order or regulation made under the authority of this act, shall be deemed not to be an abrogation, abridgement, or infringement of any right or freedom recognized by the Canadian bill of rights".
Then subsection (2)-and this is the amendment:
(2) No Canadian citizen may be deported from Canada under this act.
We know that in the not too distant past action has been taken under the War Measures Act which resulted in the deportation of Canadian citizens. I have said previously, and I do not mind repeating it, that I think it was unfortunate that that was done, and I hope in similar circumstances it would not be done again and this amendment would make it impossible to do it.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I hope that this amendment, which would prevent this kind of thing in any circumstances, the deportation or driving out of Canada of Canadian citizens, will commend itself to the committee.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the
Leader of the Opposition has pointed out that in 1947, among other things, I stated that I believed the time had come for the repeal of the War Measures Act. I remember very well holding that view and it received no support at that time, and that was within a year and a half after the United Nations had been set up at San Francisco. Canadians, as were free men all over the world, were of the opinion that the possibility of another war taking place was remote, if indeed such a possibility existed at all. We believed at that time that we had entered upon a new era where peace would become the universal way of mankind. Indeed, I am one of those who having heard Mr. Molotov at San Francisco in 1945 believed that that would indeed be the course which mankind would take. Events since have shown that the hopes of mankind have not been completely justified, and I think that statement is a major understatement.
I remember many years ago being in the gallery of the House of Commons-I cannot now place the year, and I have not Hansard before me

but I recall the late Ernest Lapointe saying that the War Measures Act was no longer in effect. He said it was still on the statute books but it was not in effect. My recollection is that at that time he, or someone else speaking during the course of the discussion in this regard, indicated that the law officers of the crown had given that opinion.
The War Measures Act is a measure which, of course, was adopted just prior to the outbreak of the second world war. It is well to

refer to the powers contained in that act. It authorized the governor in council:
-to do and authorize such acts and things and make from time to time such orders and regulations as he may by reason of the existence of real or apprehended war, invasion or insurrection deem necessary or advisable for the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada, and for greater certainty among other powers are-
And the powers mentioned include censorship, arrest, detention, exclusion and deportation, control of the harbours, ports and territorial waters of Canada and the movement of vessels, transportation, trading, exportation, importation, production and manufacture, appropriation, control, forfeiture and disposition of property and the use thereof. Then the rights of the individual are greatly diminished by section 5 which reads:
No person who is held for deportation under this act or under any regulation made thereunder or who is under arrest or detention as an alien enemy or upon suspicion that he is an alien enemy, or to prevent his departure from Canada shall be released on bail or otherwise discharged or tried without the consent of the Minister of Justice.
Those are wide and terrifying powers when considered in the light of the rights of free men. However, it has been recognized by all political parties that during the days of war the rights of the individual are placed in pawn, as it were, as security against the day of victory.
I had the opportunity during the days of war to serve on the defence committee set up on the defence of Canada regulations. It was a committee, as I recall, of some eight or nine members and it was one which gave those of us who were privileged to serve on it an opportunity of seeing the operation of the War Measures Act.
One recalls the internment of numbers of Canadians who in the light of subsequent events were as innocent of wrongdoing as any hon. member of this house. They were taken into custody. I am not going to mention names, but there is one outstanding Canadian of Italian origin who spent a considerable period in an internment camp and, who, upon examination of the record, including the confidential and secret record, by any fair-minded man should not have been interned. Indeed, upon the record as I saw it that man was as innocent as it is possible for anyone to be. But there was the finger of suspicion. Accepted was the chit chat and hearsay of others. Wrongs took place, justified though they were because of the exigencies of war.
The same condition of affairs applied in the United Kingdom under the defence of the realm regulations. Indeed, the record of two
Human Rights
world wars is replete with examples of injustices done to our fellow men, not intentionally but none the less actually.
What shall we do with regard to the War Measures Act? The Leader of the Opposition has mentioned that Canadians were subject to deportation. He said that those orders in council were passed under the War Measures Act. I think the original ones were and I speak subject to correction when I state that I believe the subsequent orders were passed under the Emergency Powers Act or under the Transitional Powers Act, whichever was the successor to the War Measures Act following the war. The effect was to go further than deportation. I have a copy of the original order in council in my hand dated December 15, 1945, P.C. 7356. It reads, in part, as follows:
Whereas by order in council P.C. 7355 of 15th December, 1945, provision is made for the deportation of persons who, during the course of the war, have requested to be removed or sent to an enemy country or otherwise manifested their sympathy with or support of the enemy powers and have by such actions shown themselves to be unfit for permanent residence in Canada;
Therefore, His Excellency the Governor General in Council is pleased to order and doth hereby order as follows:
1. Any person who, being a British subject by naturalization under the Naturalization Act, chapter 138. R.S.C. 1927, is deported from Canada under the provisions of order in council P.C. 7355 of 15th December, 1945, shall, as and from the date upon which he leaves Canada in the course of such deportation, cease to be either a British subject or a Canadian national.
I am not going to go back over those days but certainly the only offence that many of these people committed was their colour. There was no evidence against them of wrongdoing that would have stood up for a moment in any court of law had they had the opportunity to appear in a court of law.
The War Measures Act either in its present form or, better still, in an amended form must remain in effect under the trying and dangerous times in which we live. We have behind us the experience of two world wars. I believe that this measure deserves the fullest study on the part of hon. members of parliament and at the earliest possible date. I suggest that while it has been in effect since 1914 the experience of two world wars justifies amendments being made which will not sacrifice security but will to the highest degree possible maintain the fundamental rights of the individual in Canada.
How to bring about that condition of affairs has tried the minds of thinkers throughout the years. I believe that if the house is agreeable we should at the next session set up a special committee representative of all parts of the house, not on a party basis whatever, for the purpose of giving the fullest consideration to this whole question

Human Rights
of maintaining security while at the same time assuring a maximum of freedom for the rights of the individual. If a committee is set up and, of course, I am in the hands of the house as always-
The right hon. gentleman has some influence.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend for those kind words. His geniality has brought about the recognition of a fact that he often denies.
This would be a most important contribution to the Canada of today and to the Canada of the future. At that time we would not deal as we are asked to now on a piecemeal basis with the rights under the War Measures Act. If there is a degree of unanimity, and I think there will be, that Canadian citizens should not be deported the committee might make that recommendation along with such other recommendations as will bring about a War Measures Act which on the one hand will maintain the solidarity and security of the state and on the other hand will have before it the paramount necessity of not needlessly sacrificing the rights of Canadians. I suggest, therefore, that particularizing one incident in the bill of rights would not be beneficial or helpful.
Many other things were done under the War Measures Act with which I will not deal in detail. It was sometimes used as a means whereby the executive could circumvent parliament and do those things that were unjustified, unreasonable and unconscionable. In short, I suggest this. We have by the amendment to clause 6, as suggested, assured parliamentary control which has not previously existed under the War Measures Act. We have provided that the particular clauses I referred to in general shall come into force only upon the issue of a proclamation; that this proclamation shall be laid before parliament forthwith after its issue or, if parliament is then not sitting, within the first 15 days next thereafter when parliament is sitting; and that where a proclamation has been laid before parliament a notice of motion in either house signed by 10 members thereof and made in accordance with the rules of that house within 10 days of the day the proclamation was laid before parliament, praying that the proclamation be revoked, shall be debated in that house at the first convenient opportunity.
In other words we do not intend to ask in this country again to be endowed with absolute power, power above the courts in most cases, without having the authority of parliament. That is of the essence of the parliamentary system. If the cabinet can proceed to bring into effect a system of absolute
IMr. Diefenbaker.]
power for itself, that of itself constitutes a dangerous probability for the rights of the individual. We suggest immediately that we shall reduce forthwith the power to make ourselves absolute as a cabinet if we are in power when war comes, which I hope will never come about. Whatever other government is in power then will have to come to parliament and ask the representatives of the people whether they will confirm the grant to the cabinet of absolute power.
Then as to the War Measures Act and the particulars as to the removal of needless powers, that is a question, as I see it, for consideration by itself. Personally I have felt, and I am unchanged in that view, that the War Measures Act deserves the most careful analysis to the end that any powers contained therein which, in the light of experience, ought not to be possessed, should be deleted from the act. Therefore, I believe that simply to take one of the absolute powers which all of us look back at today, which brought about the exile of Canadians without trial, without offence proved, not even suspicion as a basis for proof, and it could never be accepted as such, is not what we should do. We should not in a bill of rights specifically take one of the absolute powers away without having given the fullest consideration to all of the powers in the War Measures Act. After that has been done, then it will be early enough to single out one of the absolute powers to the exclusion of all others.
Under these circumstances, with feelings of antagonism against the operation of the War Measures Act as it is capable of being exercised and was exercised, I believe that our action should be taken on the whole act and therefore it would be unfortunate if we should now start to single out one of the items which we regard to have been a tyrannical exercise of power. We should rather cover the whole field and make an amendment to that act in consequence of the recommendations made by a representative committee at the next session.

Mr. Chairman, we have all listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks just made by the Prime Minister. As far as I am concerned, I can say that I listened with a great deal of appreciation of some of the aspects upon which he touched. Naturally, I am most interested in all phases and policies of this bill of rights, but I do have a particular interest in this clause, and I have not yet heard anything to make me change my opinion that the Leader of the Opposition has moved a most worth-while amendment. The new clause 6A(1) says:
(1)	Subject to subsection 2, any act or thing done or authorized or any order or regulation

made under the authority of this act, shall be deemed not to be an abrogation, abridgement, or infringement of any right or freedom recognized by the Canadian bill of rights.
(2)	No Canadian citizen may be deported from Canada under this act.
We in this group cannot help but remember the situation when Japan entered world war II. In Canada we had thousands of Canadian citizens of Japanese origin. Thousands of them were born in Canada; they did not know any other country but Canada and the principles espoused by Canada. And yet, under the act which was mentioned here, those who were citizens of Canada but not of our colour or racial origin were within 24 hours cut from their homes, from their houses, their businesses, their property and put in camps and then dispersed across Canada. At that time I had the honour of being the leader of the opposition in the province of British Columbia and I can still remember not one, but dozens of people representing hundreds of Japanese Canadians, citizens, coming to my office and pleading for the right to fight on behalf of Canada in any way that Canada wanted, in a combatant force, a labour battalion on any front, and yet they were denied.
Following the cessation of hostilities I was interested in checking as far as I could under security measures on what happened, and the answer was that there was not one solitary incident or instance of insubordination or of any act of sabotage by those Canadian citizens. At the same time we were the only voice that was raised on behalf of Canadian citizens, irrespective of their land of origin or of their colour. We were the only voice raised at that time which said that every Canadian citizen was entitled to a vote. How we were condemned and damned because we believed in Canadian citizenship and only one kind of citizenship. Today everyone has the vote. I noticed in the press only last week that the Conservative party has named a Japanese Canadian as a candidate in the next provincial election in British Columbia. How times do change.
In view of that episode, unfortunate as it was, we think and I have listened to the Prime Minister and I think he agrees with those views also-that there should be something in the bill of rights in time of peace or war which says that a Canadian citizen is a loyal Canadian citizen unless he is found guilty of betrayal or sabotage aginst the Dominion of Canada. I am not going to say any more. It is now six o'clock and I do not want to carry on afterward. It is for that reason that I find myself very sympathetic toward many of the words that the
Human Rights
Prime Minister has used and also most sympathetic toward the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition.
Six o'clock.
Do you want to go right through?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, the Prime Minister in response to the suggestions made by the Leader of the Opposition reminded us of the words of the late minister ot justice, the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe. I do not comment on that fact, except to observe that this morning the Prime Minister admonished me for quoting from observations made by one who is deceased.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: That was right in Hansard.
I would remind the Prime Minister that he quoted the words of a man who was likewise deceased.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: That was right in Hansard.
That has nothing to do with the bill but it seems to me the sort of response-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: One set of words is recorded and the other set was supposed to be a private conversation.
Now the Minister of Justice adds pearls of wisdom that do not really help the situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am glad you recognize them for what they are.

The Prime Minister did not deny that he had urged at one time, not this particular amendment to the War Measures Act, but a much wider application in revision of the War Measures Act. One can only suspect it is because he is now sitting to Mr. Speaker's right, that he takes a position somewhat less liberal toward this act in relation to the question of a bill of rights than he formerly took. He suggests that next year we might have an opportunity of studying the War Measures Act in relation to the bill of rights and on its own account, and that at that time it would be more appropriate to consider the amendment offered by the Leader of the Opposition.

Human Rights
I must tell the Prime Minister that I find his attitude a little surprising, particularly in view of his well known views which, as he reminded us this morning, he has expressed often in the house and outside. It is difficult to reconcile these general observations with his suggestion that we postpone this amendment, which in any event I am sure would be agreed upon in any revision of the War Measures Act, until next year. It would seem to me that any examination of the amendment proposed by the Leader of the Opposition will reveal that, revision or no revision, there would be general agreement in the house on this amendment which basically provides that no Canadian citizen may be deported from Canada under this act.
We are talking now of the Canadian citizen. We are not talking of any other individual in our country except a Canadian citizen, and we are saying that under the War Measures Act such a person should not be deported. We are not saying that the bill of rights should supersede the War Measures Act. We are all cognizant of the requirements of security in time of war, but we recognize this as a minimum kind of liberalization. It would seem to me that when we are discussing a bill of rights this minimum kind of liberalization should be contemporary with the passing of the bill of rights.
The Prime Minister, however, has refused to accept this on the grounds that there will be a complete revision later on. This we cannot accept, and I would suggest to the Prime Minister that if he would read the evidence of Professor Lower, one of his great champions and admirers, he will find that on interrogation by me Professor Lower agreed with this amendment. It is true, that after I had interrogated Professor Lower in the committee, having to leave to come to the house to attend to my obligations here, because of the way in which the business of the house was managed, compelling us to move from the committee to the house, I was faced with the situation that did not allow me to deal with Professor Lower when he was being examined in my absence, not by a member of the committee, but by one who, in terms of interrogation, was there by courtesy, namely my friend the Minister of Justice. The Minister of Justice interrogated Professor Lower after I had gone-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I did not get a chance to get a word in edgeways while you were there.

-and it is an
indication of the flexibility of Professor Lower, that the Minister of Justice was able to elicit from the distinguished professor from Queen's University precisely opposite

answers to those which I had been able to elicit when the Minister of Justice remained quiet. But I must say that this flexibility was not contagious, because the Minister of Justice has not revealed any such ability until the very late hours of this afternoon, a flexibility which we all accept and recognize and for which we are grateful.
The Prime Minister gave us a dissertation on the problems of security. He told us about how important the War Measures Act was in the event of war. I am sure we appreciated this recital of the importance of the War Measures Act by the Prime Minister, but it seems to me that that recital was part of the Prime Minister's well known technique of diversion. It was not addressed to the amendment, and the Prime Minister at no time said that the amendment was an unacceptable one. The only argument he adduced was that it should not be accepted at this time because it was hoped that at the next session there would be an examination of the War Measures Act, when that act could be viewed in its totality.
The Prime Minister will not misunderstand me when I say that since 1957 we have had too many examples of this technique of postponement. I need only refer to the experience of the western liaison committee in the matter of postponement. We could easily be faced with a situation next session, if there is going to be one, that the Prime Minister would find some reason why the War Measures Act could not be discussed at that time. In any event, the fact is we are pressing this point under the War Measures Act that no Canadian citizen should be deported from Canada. One could easily put the question, where would one deport a Canadian citizen? No country would be obliged to take a Canadian citizen.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: You did not find that difficult in 1946.
What was the case in 1946 to which the Prime Minister refers?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The Japanese.

Oh, I see now. I just had a heavy dinner, and I am not as quick as usual. All I can say is that the situation to which the Prime Minister directs my attention was one which elicited very strong support for the government of the day by the hon. gentleman sitting on the Prime Minister's right, the Minister of Justice, and the hon. gentleman seated on his left, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who said we did not go far enough.
The point is, are we, in a bill of rights, to say we are not going to accord to any Canadian citizen the limits [DOT] which are provided

by this amendment? The Prime Minister said that we must revise the War Measures Act next year or some time in the future. Then he went on to tell us about the revision which the government itself was making in the War Measures Act. If the argument is sound that we should not discuss now any revision of the War Measures Act, why was it not sound for the government itself to amend the War Measures Act in the bill of rights? The Prime Minister did not find it difficult to do, what we ourselves tried to do. He reminded us of the liberalization which he and his government is supposed to have effected in the amendment of the War Measures Act as provided in clause 6 of this bill.
I must say, that passing over this display of lack of consistency on the part of the right hon. gentleman, I cannot agree that the amendments which he has provided is substantial. What is that amendment? He says in clause 6 (2):
A proclamation declaring that war, invasion or insurrection, real or apprehended, exists shall be laid before parliament forthwith after its issue, or, if parliament is then not sitting, within the first fifteen days next thereafter that parliament is sitting.
I will admit that is, in form, a liberalization. I will recognize that is an amendment to the War Measures Act. It is suggested that the amendment, which we have proposed should be postponed until the total revision takes place. However, a revision that the government makes is, of course, in an altogether different category. I submit the Prime Minister should not be too gleeful or enthusiastic about the amendment he has provided for in clause 6 (2) because it is really meaningless. The fact is that parliament, at any time under the existing War Measures Act, has the opportunity to discuss a proclamation declaring that war, invasion or insurrection, real or apprehended, exists. This was never denied parliament, and was always a right that parliament had. If the Prime Minister thinks I am exaggerating when I make that statement, let me call as my witness no less a person than the Minister of Justice himself. At pages 584 and 585 of the committee evidence the Minister of Justice is reported as saying:
If you did that, of course, then the effect would be that it could be debated not only shortly after the proclamation, or alternatively, shortly after parliament met, but at any time thereafter This would happen if you cut that limitation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You remember I amended those remarks later.

My hon. friend says he amended that. I am not aware that he did amend those words, but it seems to me they are rather inconsequential and any amendment would be meaningless. However,
Human Rights
if he did I make note of it. What I am coming to now is the important part of what the minister said:
I would like to point out that from the point of view of an administration, the urgency of taking out the War Measures Act is, it is true, not as great as the urgency for bringing it into effect; but on the other hand, parliament could always debate it in any event, or discuss it in debate on the throne speech, on the estimates of the Department of National Defence, for instance, on supply motions, and by attacking the regulations tabled in the House of Commons under the War Measures Act as an encroachment of the provisions of the Regulations Act, and by various other methods. What we have thought important to ensure is that parliament should have the right to challenge the declaration of emergency itself in order that parliament should have the right to raise the question of whether it is not a false emergency brought in or created for the purpose of enabling the government to get around the bill of rights.
I was about to quote my own pearls of wisdom, but they do not add anything except to corroborate the generality involved in the statement of the Minister of Justice, which I find so helpful at this time. There need not be anything else said. The Prime Minister's argument has been discredited by his own Minister of Justice. He has indicated the inconsequential character of the amendment which the Prime Minister and his government have proposed in clause 6 (2), but in the very fact that they have proposed an amendment they have justified the amendment proposed by the Leader of the Opposition. As I say, this amendment involves the minimum kind of thing one would do in the liberalization of the War Measures Act, in an effort to give that measure of protection to the citizen which is consistent with security demands and with what is contained in the bill of rights.
The Prime Minister has not offered any substantial argument of which I could possibly conceive, that would stand in the way of the acceptance of this amendment. It is an amendment that would warm the heart of that great admirer of his, the author of the book "From Colony to Nation", Professor Lower, who spoke of the Prime Minister in most generous terms. If not for me, I hope that in the interests of satisfying Professor Lower the Prime Minister will accept this amendment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: I am glad to have those words from the hon. gentleman who paid Professor Lower such a high tribute, with which of course I entirely concur. Having had Professor Lower designated by the hon. gentleman as a worthy man whose suggestions and ideas should be followed, may I quote from the bottom of page 331 of the committee evidence:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Would you then agree with me that it is a sensible provision at the moment to put

Human Rights
this safeguard in against abuses of the powers of invoking the War Measures Act,-
That is the particular matter covered by clause 6.
-which will thus give you some protection against the abuse of powers conferred by the act; and then say we will look next at the act to see whether improvements should be made in the statute itself.
Professor Lower then stated:
Yes, I was under the impression, when I read this, that this is an attempt to make criticism of the War Measures Act. From what you say about it I can see you have something additional in mind. I would be very happy not only to have this retained but also to have the revision of the War Measures Act make subsequently. Of course, I do think it is too big a thing to be examined at this time of year.
So I entirely accept the designation of Professor Lower's capacity and ability, the evidence which he gave, and simply quote, in answer to the hon. gentleman, the words of Professor Lower.

Mr. Chairman, I was struck by one remark in particular which the Prime Minister made when he spoke before the dinner hour. He used this expression which I jotted down: The executive can circumvent parliament if it desires-if it wishes. I do not know what the Prime Minister meant when he said that the executive can circumvent parliament. Surely the members of the house can be really concerned about the possibility that the executive, the cabinet, can circumvent parliament. If we look at clause 6, paragraph Cl) it states:
Sections 3, 4 and 5 shall come Into force only upon the issue of a proclamation of the governor in council declaring that war, invasion or insurrection, real or apprehended, exists.
Then paragraph (2) states:
A proclamation declaring that war, invastion or insurrection, real or apprehended, exists shall be laid before parliament forthwith after its issue, or, if parliament is then not sitting, within the first fifteen days next thereafter that parliament is sitting.
Strangely enough there is no precaution taken in this clause that parliament should promptly be convened. If the executive desires, for example, to wait for the full term of 12 months to expire from the last date that parliament sat it is conceivable that the executive could then run the country for 11 months; that is, if we suppose that the declaration of war was made one month after parliament prorogued. Perhaps there is something in that, that during these 11 months the executive will not be able to place before parliament the declaration of war so that parliament can discuss it, and perhaps that could be one of the ways in which parliament could be circumvented for at least 11 months.

I would therefore suggest, or invite the Prime Minister's consideration to this inclusion in paragraph (2), that if the declaration should be presented to parliament within 15 days next thereafter that parliament is sitting-those 15 days can be, as I said, 11 months hence-and I wonder whether it would not be wiser, or a greater precaution to safeguard our rights and deal with the emergency so that parliament can deal with it and not the executive alone, for the Prime Minister to include that parliament should be-I am not offering this as an amendment; but merely as a suggestion-convened say, within a month after the declaration, or within 15 days, depending upon the emergency.
I think in that way in times of emergency parliament can be certain that it will be convened to pass upon and to deal with a dangerous situation or a proclamation which the governor in council may have made. If we have that limitation, that parliament cannot just be circumvented during months at a time, I think the people of Canada, and parliament certainly, would be given the opportunity which it is entitled to have, and therefore perhaps eliminate a possibility that parliament might be circumvented by the executive.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
On that point, Mr. Chairman, I would simply make the observation that I do not think the house itself would want to impose upon any government an obligation which, upon reflection, it realized that the government might very well not be able to discharge. If there should be a war-which, as the Prime Minister has said, everyone here hopes there will not be-of a nuclear or atomic nature, it simply might not be physically possible to call parliament within 15 days of the outbreak; everything might be in a state of complete physical chaos. We would have liked to put in some time within which parliament must be called; but we felt we could not do any better, because of that possibility, than leave in the provision of the British North America Act which imposes upon the government the constitutional responsibility of having a session at least once a year.
Amendment (Mr. Pearson) negatived: Yeas, 25; nays, 72.

Mr. Chairman, the Prime Minister will perhaps be relieved to note that this is perhaps the last amendment on the operative part of the bill; but it is, on that account, not less in substance than any of the ones that have preceded it. I move,

seconded by the hon. member for Maison-neuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets):
That subsection (5) of section 6 of clause 6 be deleted and that there be added the following
section as section 6A:
"6A (1) Subject to subsections 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 any act or thing done or authorized or any order or regulation made under the authority of this act, shall be deemed not to be an abrogation, abridgement, or infringement of any right or freedom recognized by the Canadian bill of rights.
(2) No naturalized Canadian citizen may be deprived of his citizenship and no naturalized British subject may be deprived of his status as a British subject under this act.
(3)	No Canadian citizen or British subject may be detained under this act beyond a period of sixty days, unless the cause for his detention has been reviewed by an appropriate impartial tribunal which has reported to the minister or the authorities authorizing the detention.
(4) Any order or regulation under this act conferring authority to order the detention of any person shall, forthwith after it is made, be laid before parliament, or if parliament is not then sitting, within the first fifteen days next thereafter that parliament is sitting.
(5)	Where an order or regulation has been laid before parliament pursuant to subsection (4), a notice of motion in either house, signed by ten members thereof, and made in accordance with the rules of that house within ten days of the day the order or regulation was laid before parliament, praying that the order or regulation be revoked, shall be debated in that house at the first convenient opportunity within the four sitting days next after the day the motion in the house was made.
(6)	If either house of parliament resolve pursuant to a motion made under subsection (5) that the order or regulation be revoked, it shall cease to have effect, without prejudice, to the previous operation of the order or regulation, or anything duly done thereunder.
The observations which were made by the Leader of the Opposition in proposing the previous amendment, and my response to those of the Prime Minister when he commented on that amendment would, it seems to me, apply to this particular amendment which I recommend to the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In general the remarks made by the Prime Minister apply to this amendment, namely that what is sought to be done here is to suggest particular ways in which the War Measures Act should be amended. The Prime Minister has given an assurance that the War Measures Act will be placed under review at the first convenient opportunity, at which time all the features of that act will be reviewed by parliament or by a committee of parliament so that it may then be determined what it is that should be changed. I bring as a witness in support of the contention that that is the proper way in which to do it, Professor Lower himself, who agreed in reply to a question by me that the War Measures Act is much too big a subject to get into at this time of the year. In other words, Professor Lower was agreeing that when we are considering a bill of rights at
Human Rights
this stage and in this context it is not an appropriate time to consider amending the War Measures Act in particular but that that project should be left to the kind of examination which the Prime Minister has indicated will be undertaken.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The position of the government on this matter has been made quite clear. They are willing to put into the bill of rights their own amendment to the War Measures Act, and though we say this is some improvement it is a very inconsequential improvement, as was pointed out by nearly all the witnesses in the special committee. But when we move amendments which would put some teeth in the protection afforded, the government says it will defer consideration to some future time. We have to accept that decision of the government, but it is not a very impressive one.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Let me make this very clear. In so far as this is concerned, no naturalized Canadian may be deprived of his citizenship and no naturalized British subject may be deprived of his status as a British subject under this act, and we accept that as a desirable objective when full and complete amendment of the War Measures Act or other acts is made. If my memory serves me right, the last case of their being a deprivation of citizenship and also a deprivation of the status of British subject was under the order in council in 1945 and again in 1946. I am very glad that hon. gentlemen opposite in the light of the perspective of reconsideration now agree that the course then followed was a wrong one. That is all to the good. Furthermore, no Canadian citizen or British subject must be detained under this act beyond a period of 60 days unless the case for his detention has been reviewed by an appropriate impartial tribunal which has reported to the minister or the authority authorizing the detention. Nothing could have been more conducive to injustice than the regulations that were in effect during the last war whereby men were interned without any opportunity being given to them of understanding the charge against them, denied, as they were in 1946, the right to have counsel.
I am not bringing these things up in order to recall the past but simply to point out that we at that time took the strongest objection, and we are glad we are now joined by those opposite who in those days disregarded our warnings and our request for action in this connection. I can assure hon. gentlemen opposite that this is the type of thing that will not again happen in this country.
We do not want to precipitate, unconsidered, piecemeal consideration of the War Measures Act, and it is for that reason these particular

Human Rights
matters can best be dealt with in detail by a committee. Indeed, it has been made very clear by hon. gentlemen opposite that as a result of a committee which has met in connection with a bill of rights improvements have been brought forward, and I know that at the next session, if the house agrees to set up such a committee as I have proposed, we shall be able in co-operation and with a common dedication to remove and eradicate those things that bring shame to our hearts today as we think of some of the things that were done in the past.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The Prime Minister has now said that these are good amendments, that he approves of them and that at some time in the future they may be put into effect. The Prime Minister and his government have been considering this bill of rights now for two and a half years. They found time during those years to introduce one change in the War Measures Act and at some time in the future they will put into effect the other changes that are so good. Such is the process of procrastination.
I wish to say briefly that this party, the only party in the house with a clear record and conscience on this question -nobody can deny that; I challenge anyone to question that statement right now-
Do you have a conscience?

As the only party with a clear record and conscience on this question we support the principle of this amendment. However, I am rather surprised to find such a distinguished colleague as the hon. member for Essex East writing an amendment in what I consider to be a somewhat loose form. On page 2 of the amendment I read, in lines 5 and 6 "four sitting days after the day the motion in the house was made". I always understood that a motion was moved and not made in this house.

I thank the hon. member for his editorial support. We all would have been very happy in the Liberal party if throughout the discussions at this stage of the debate we had had the active support of the hon. gentleman and his colleagues in connection with these substantive measures.
I regret that the Prime Minister, accepting the principle of this amendment, has not agreed to put it in the bill of rights. I should like to have seen this adopted not next year but today.
Amendment (Mr. Martin, Essex East) negatived: Yeas, 28; nays, 84.
Clause 6 agreed to.
On the preamble.

Mr. Chairman, 1 take it the only matter before the committee now is the preamble. The preamble which was proposed by the Leader of the Opposition in spite of the criticism levelled at the idea is now before us. It represents a composite effort provided for by the law officers of the Department of Justice. We have no objection to the first paragraph which reads:
The parliament of Canada, affirming that the Canadian nation is founded upon principles that acknowledge the supremacy of God, the dignity and worth of the human person and the position of the family in a society of free men and free institutions;
Nor is there any objection to the second paragraph which reads:
Affirming also that men and institutions remain free only when freedom is founded upon respect for moral and spiritual values and the rule of law;
I will read the third paragraph so the committee will get the sense of it and then suggest to the Minister of Justice that the tenses in that paragraph are perhaps inaccurate. It reads:
And being desirous of enshrining these principles and the human rights and fundamental freedoms derived from them, in a bill of rights which shall reflect the respect of parliament for the provisions of its constitutional authority and which shall ensure the protection of these rights and freedoms in Canada;
I suggest to the minister that instead of saying, "shall reflect" a better way of employing the correct tense would be to say "reflects" leaving out "shall"; and, in the second last line, instead of saying "shall ensure" the correct usage would be "ensures". I believe that would be a more correct representation of the tense. I propose that simply by way of a suggestion.
However, I would formally move that in the twelfth line the word "provision" be deleted after the word "the" and that there be substituted therefor the word "limits". That would bring the English text into full conformity with the meaning as provided for in the French text which reads as follows: (Translation) :
And being desirous of enshrining these principles and the human rights and fundamental freedoms derived from them, in a bill of rights which shall reflect the respect of parliament for the provisions of its constitutional authority and which shall ensure the protection of these rights and freedoms in Canada:
(Text):
I formally move:
That the word "provisions" in the twelfth line be deleted and that there be substituted therefor the word "limits".

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on the proposals made by the hon. member for Essex East I am very glad indeed to have this opportunity of indicating a degree of flexibility which I am quite sure will surprise the hon. gentleman in view of some of the strictures

he has heaped upon me. I refer particularly to the question of the word "provisions" for which the hon. member suggests we substitute the word "limits".
I think the committee will be interested to know that when I first drafted the preamble which was submitted to the special committee and out of which this present agreed form came-and I drafted it on the basis of all the suggestions that had been made and then had a draft prepared in the department; I took that and prepared the final form in which it was submitted to the special committee- I had originally used the word "limits" instead of "provisions". Then, being flexible, I dicussed this with some hon. members and others who were interested and they suggested that possibly the word "limits" would be interpreted as meaning that parliament had enacted a limited bill of rights, that parliament had sort of shrunk a little bit and not enacted a broad and generous measure; so they said, not because of the technical sense of the word but because of the poetic implications or the implications in the sense of language, maybe it would not be desirable to use the word "limits" and it was suggested to me that we use the word "provisions" instead which would be unobjectionable from that point of view.
Desirous of demonstrating a degree of flexibility and readiness to accept all reasonable suggestions that come from anywhere as long as they did not destroy the effect and intent of the bill, I said "All right, we will take out 'limits' and put in 'provisions' ", and therefore when it was submitted to the special committee it contained the word "provisions".
The draft preamble as submitted was worked over. I would remind the committee and the hon. member for Essex East that in the form in which it now appears in this reprinted bill it was approved unanimously by the special committee. We now find the hon. member for Essex East suggesting with the most perfect sincerity and constructive thought that the word "provisions" should be deleted and the word "limits" substituted and also that the two "shalls" shall be taken out. Again I am desirous of demonstrating that degree of flexibility which the hon. member has suggested I do not always show. I am prepared to agree with his suggestion with regard to that particular word, but I think surely that by this complete 100 degree circle, if you like-
Circles have 360 degrees.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
-I have succeeded in demonstrating for all time my readiness to be flexible and to accommodate the views of hon. members. Personally I have no strong feelings about whether the word "provisions"
Human Rights
or "limits" is used. Possibly the word "limits" is more precise; I think the word "provisions" is more poetic and in discussing whether a word should be poetic or not, again I think I indicated a degree of flexibility.
I think, Mr. Chairman, this is one of those problems where it should be left to the judgment of the committee. I would suggest there is no point in taking a firm stand as a representative of the government on whether it be "limits" or "provisions". I have some personal preference now for the word "provisions", for the reasons that first of all prevailed upon me to put in the word "provisions". In this respect I would suggest that it be left to the judgment of the committee of the whole house. The hon. member has moved a motion to substitute for the word "provisions" the word "limits". If that commends itself to the committee, I shall be perfectly happy. If, on the other hand, the judgment of the committee is that in the circumstances the word "provisions" is the better word, then again I think we shall all be perfectly happy.
Will my hon. friend second my motion?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No; I will not do that because I prefer to leave this to the judgment of the committee uninfluenced by my personal opinion as to what is the better word for the purpose that we are trying to achieve here.
But with regard to the elimination suggested by the hon. member of the two words "shall", here I know he has not moved an amendment, but I do have some fairly strong views. I think the word "shall" is more prospective; it brings attention more to what is to follow; it indicates that parliament now is desirous of doing this thing and parliament will do those things which shall reflect its respect of the provisions of its own constitutional authority and shall ensure protection of those rights and freedoms in Canada. Of course, although we have merely the future tense, or an expression of determination as to what shall be done, the bill itself still commences to be operative and effective from the moment that it is enacted. Therefore, there is no disadvantage from that point of view in having the words "shall" in the preamble. I think they are indicative of a conscientious determination on the part of parliament, and it is desirable that they should be in the preamble for that purpose.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I simply say with respect to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Essex East, as far as the government is concerned, it is prepared to leave to the judgment of the committee whether the word "provisions" or the word "limits" is preferable.

Human Rights
With regard to the preamble as a whole, may I take advantage of this opportunity to say that it was the unanimous recommendation of the special committee that the preamble should be in this form. As we draw near to the close of our deliberations in committee I wish to say that I think the special committee, as well as the committee of the whole house, has produced a bill of rights for all Canadians which is as expressive as the House of Commons and parliament would desire it to be of those principles with respect to the basic rights and fundamental freedoms upon which our whole existence as a body politic depends, of which this parliament may be proud, for which I know this nation will be grateful to the Prime Minister for his continuous, conscientious and successful efforts to give to the Canadian nation a bill of rights upon which it will find a firm anchor for its democratic freedoms.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, notwithstanding that the discussion of this bill has from time to time been sharp-this is not an altogether undesirable feature when we concern ourselves with those things which go to the very warp and woof of our corporative existence as a nation; obviously, men feel keenly about these things, and members of parliament particularly feel most keenly about them-notwithstanding that there have occasionally been sharp differences of opinion expressed in the discussion in committee of the whole, I believe that the House of Commons can be proud, and every individual member of the House of Commons can be proud, of the part that this house has played in these discussions, and will I am certain pay a tribute to the Prime Minister and the government of which he is head for having provided the occasion for this discussion and will take a sense of pride and proper gratification, tempered with proper humility, in the achievement that this House of Commons has brought about.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May X draw to the attention of the Minister of Justice one matter which I think he may not have given attention to, namely that if the preamble, particularly the last paragraph which has been brought to the attention of the committee by the hon. member for Essex East, remains as it is in both texts, then the third paragraph in the French bill and the third paragraph in the English bill will have a different meaning. I do not think there is any doubt about that if you look at the words:
(Translation):
.. .in a bill of rights which shall reflect the respect of parliament for the provisions of its constitutional authority...

(Text) :
Which is translated as follows:
-a bill of rights which shall reflect the respect of parliament for the provisions of its constitutional authority-
These words, with all due respect, do not mean the same in the two bills.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Would the hon. gentleman allow a question? I am not presuming to suggest that the question I am asking is a solution of the problem, but if the words "the provisions of" were left out, would that not cover the situation. It would then read:
*-which shall reflect the respect of parliament for its constitutional authority and which shall ensure-
Would that not have the effect of achieving a solution of the difficulty mentioned by the hon. gentleman?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I would not like to answer no to that, but I would like to say this: the French version uses the word "limits" which is extremely important in the English translation. My understanding is that the translation has been from the French to the English.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Or vice versa. There is no doubt, whether it is from the one to the other, unless the word "limits" is put in the English text it will not have the same meaning as the French text, because the French text clearly states that it is the limits of the legislative competence of parliament which is emphasized. That is why I think the word "limits" should be substituted for the word "provisions".

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
May I follow up the Prime Minister's suggestion very briefly. The Prime Minister's suggestion is that we solve what might be a dilemma or an impasse by deleting from the English text "the provisions of" so that it would then read:
-the respect of parliament for its constitutional authority-
In the French text the same purpose may be achieved by deleting the three words "les limites de", so that the French version would then read:
-qui respecte la competence legislative du par-lement-
I think the same result would be achieved in both versions by the elimination of these three words and the impasse might therefore be resolved without the necessity of any division of opinion.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure we are grateful to the Prime Minister for his efforts in trying to resolve what is recognized by all of us as a very desirable and important decision as we deal with this

matter in its final stage. To say "which shall reflect the respect of parliament for its constitutional authority" does not meet the point that we had in mind in putting in any reference to the constitutional authority. What we were seeking to establish was that there are certain matters that reside outside the competence of parliament, and if we simply say "respect of parliament for its constitutional authority" we do not thereby imply that there is a division of powers, and that is the very thing we want to do so as not to offend any provincial powers. I suggest that the idea the minister had originally of putting in the word "limits" as it is in the French is the most satisfactory way of concluding the problem. Otherwise we will not be achieving in the preamble the very thing which all of us in the committee sought, a recognition of the division of powers.
You have it in clause 5.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You have it in clause 5.

It is true, as the hon. member for Essex West says, that our amendment to clause 5 was accepted this afternoon, but what we want to do is to carry out the main principle of the bill, and to leave the matter in the way it was suggested would be to ignore the very thing about which all of us in the house and the provinces as well are sensitive. We are not interested in invading their powers under section 92 and have no intention of so doing. For that reason we recognize in this preamble that the respect of parliament is for those matters that are within our constitutional authority, and I think the word "limits" sets that out very adequately.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a brief word or two on behalf of this group before discussion of the bill is concluded. We support this measure wholeheartedly as a first and important step to protect fundamental rights and human freedoms in Canada. The other day we urged that the government take every advantage of the mood of the provinces at the present time to secure agreement between the provinces and the federal government for the inclusion of a bill of rights in our constitution.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we are now discussing the preamble to the bill. I think it is a good preamble and I wish to take this opportunity to congratulate all those who worked on it and who produced this very comprehensive document. I do not know exactly who the authors of the preamble are but I believe that all members of the committee shared in the drafting, and they did a good job. Like others, Mr. Chairman, I tried my hand at drafting a preamble. I know that the Prime Minister read one
Human Rights
yesterday which was very moving in its terms. Even the hon. member for Essex East read his preamble, and it was also very good.
I did not succeed in submitting my preamble to the committee because I found as I worked on drafting it that I could not strike the right note. If I tried to be inspiring I found that I was perhaps too much so and certainly not legal enough. If I tried to be legal I found that I was legalistic to such an extent that I was far from inspiring. Be that as it may, if I may have the indulgence of members of the committee I should like to place before them my thoughts on the subject of a preamble. I am under no illusions whatsoever as to its literary merit and I also know that as a legal document it is hopelessly lacking. I probably got mixed up in all sorts of tenses and the hon. member for Essex East would surely have to move a whole series of new amendments.
However, I should like to place it before the committee as perhaps epitomizing in some sort of way the thoughts which came to me in thinking about this bill of rights which will very shortly, I hope, become the law of the land and perhaps also in some way a creed for Canadians. I beg the indulgence of the committee in putting this preamble before them:
Oh Canada, land of endless vistas, old as the rocks of time, yet fresh as the newest dawn, forged from the strange convulsions of the earth's bowels, vast, sprawling, sweeping spaces, rich and varied, offering hope and ever renewed promise.
Within these boundaries lives a diverse people, come from the many corners of the earth, of varied strains but together forming one nation, Canadians all, of whatever race, creed or colour.
They still remember ancient ties and fond attachments, but they have pledged to this country alone their mind and heart and soul. They have spread across an entire continent; freely have they taken of its bounty; joyously have they shared its precious heritage.
Country of dual culture and of many races, richly endowed, drawing strength from its very diversity, each element joining together to create a proud, independent and courageous people.
In freedom have men lived here, free to worship God in their own way, according to their conscience, free to express their opinions, to participate in public affairs, to propose changes in governments and laws, free to associate, free to lead their own lives according to their likings and to enjoy their property, restrained only by the rights of others and the general welfare, secure under a law founded on the supremacy of God and equal for all.
Freedom, true today as it was yesterday and will be tomorrow, like a fine golden thread, is the link that binds together the fabrics of this nation, that makes it live and prosper.
When freedom was threatened, Canadians rose to meet the challenge and fought the wars on freedom's side. To this cause they gave their lives because they felt that life in bondage is no life at all. And, in the darkest days their hope never faltered because they knew that freedom can never be stamped out and that, inevitably it rises again, stronger than ever from the ashes of dictators.

Human Rights
But, when the wars were over, auickly they returned to their homes and families and to the pursuit of peaceful ends. Quickly also, they forgave their enemies for they know that all men are brothers.
Clearly do they proclaim that Canada is the land of the free, but they are mindful that freedom is never quite won and eternal vigilance is its price.
Appropriate indeed and useful it is that the fundamental liberties and basic freedoms of Canadians be hereby enshrined and consecrated in a bill of rights.
Thus does the parliament of Canada, pursuant to the sovereign will of its people, solemnly seal its imperishable pact with freedom.
Will the hon. member permit a question? Is it his intention to move this as an amendment?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
I think I explained very clearly at the outset of my remarks that I had no such intention, that it was not given as a preamble but simply as an expression of faith in Canada.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, I should like to put a question to the hon. member. In view of the importance of this new document, could the hon. member immediately translate what he has just read?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: Does the hon. member want an immediate translation?
Yes, if it is possible.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Well, I drafted that document in English, and I have attempted to translate it. In fact, I have a translation. However, I did not read my French version of the preamble because, having conceived and devised it in English, I found that the rhythm of the original English version is somewhat lacking in the French translation.
(Text):

I only want to make a very brief observation at this time. I notice in the preamble the words "acknowledging the supremacy of God", and then I notice a little later on the words "affirming also that men and institutions remain free only when freedom is founded upon respect for moral and spiritual values and the rule of law". I feel very sincerely that through the ages lawmakers, whether they have been dictators or parliamentarians, have always attempted to cloak themselves with the mantle of God. I feel that the two terms may very often be contradictory, to speak of the supremacy of God and, in the same breath, attempt to identify with that supremacy the rule of law. The course of history of mankind indicates that more often than not the rule of law has not been identical with the supremacy of God. I feel this is where mankind's efforts
to establish institutions of government have so very often broken down.
There is an old saying that when Rome became Christian, the Christian church became Rome. I feel that this point is as valid today as it ever has been. I do not like this identification of the rule of law with the supremacy of God because world history ought to have taught us a few things by now. I feel that in this respect our preamble to the bill of rights has really weakened the bill. I would have preferred no preamble to this attempt to identify the rule of law with the supremacy of God, because I feel that we ought to have learned a little better than that.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I know that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has different views on this subject, but let me assure him, on behalf of all other members of the house, that I think he stands alone on this subject.
World history teaches us differently.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
However, regardless of that, we in this parliament do want to identify ourselves, and we do want to identify this bill of rights with God. We all feel that in this day of godlessness we in this nation should pride ourselves on our institutions and what they stand for, and in this instance should bring in the name of God. May I say, without any irreverence for the views expressed by the hon. member, that this is very important to us. We feel that this is one of our supreme efforts, in which all parties have joined, and we can do nothing better than couple it with God because we have found in the past, as my hon. friend must admit, that any country that has forsaken God has been very short-lived. We feel that this will be the fate of Russia and any other country that forsakes God.
May I say that I appreciate the remarks made by the hon. member for Laurier and the hon. member for Essex East concerning the contradiction in the interpretation of the word "provision" in French and in English. I do appreciate the suggestions that have been made that the word "limit" should be substituted because it means the same thing in French and in English. Looking at the Oxford dictionary we find that the word "limit" means this: the bounding line or the terminal point. Now, when you apply that to this situation, inserting the word "limit", it would not really mean what we have in mind. If we inserted those words, it would read:
And being desirous of enshrining these principles ...which shall reflect the respect of parliament for the bounding line or terminal points of its constitutional authority.

That is not what we mean at all. We mean that we are desirous of a bill of rights which shall reflect the respect of parliament for its constitutional authority, not just for the outside or extreme limits or bounding line or terminal points of the constitutional authority. If the word "limit" were inserted here as my hon. friends in the best of good faith suggest, I am respectfully suggesting we would be getting away from the principle of this bill of rights because it is not to express the limits of our constitutional authority but it is to express the respect of parliament for its constitutional authority.
My respectful submission, therefore, is that the suggestion of the Prime Minister should be accepted, namely, that the words "the provisions of" should be deleted so that the clause will now read:
And being desirous of enshrining these principles in a bill of rights... which shall reflect the respect of parliament for its constitutional authority-
Before I sit down may I say that I have been interested in this bill of rights for many years but I have not wanted to interfere in this debate which has gone so well. It has been carried on on our side by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice. I could not help but reflect with joy, and with a certain amount of satisfaction, particularly when I saw the hon. member for Essex East, not only climb on the bandwagon but almost steal the bandwagon and attempt to ride away with it. It is true that even yesterday, when he was caught out in what I would not want to call plagiarism, but simply handing out the various parts of the universal bill of rights and saying, you take this clause, you take another; this wholesale plagiarism which took place yesterday and today at least indicated that everybody is interested; even if the thoughts of the opposition are not original but came from the United Nations. Nevertheless, it is a pleasure to see that they are thinking of this subject. They have made a great contribution and, to the hon. member for Essex East, may I say this: While the lamp holds out to burn, the vilest sinner may return.

I rise at this time to protest the interpretation which the minister has placed on the remarks of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. I might say that I have too much respect for the minister's intelligence to believe that this was accidental. This was another of the minister's attempts to smear hon. members in which the minister indulges far too often.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Perhaps my hon. friend would explain that.
Human Rights

I have listened to this debate patiently ever since the Prime Minister first announced on July 1 that the bill of rights would be introduced. I had not the slightest doubt what the result would be, and it was just a question of how long it would take to pass this bill through the house.
It ran through my mind on Dominion day that this would be a very memorable day; to look at it now in a different way it would be a day for a rehearsal. As long as I can remember, on certain days in the year I have been celebrating the benefits of the bill of rights. It was passed in December, 1689, and this was emphasized all the way through the debate. I have listened to the opposition efforts to scotch every particular item of the bill of rights with no effect. Never once did they mention the name of William III, Prince of Orange who made it possible for us to be here today to enjoy the supremacy of parliament.
I was at times a little annoyed while this debate was going on with the obvious stalling, but then I went down while the debate was continuing and read some of the history of the original bill of rights just to bring myself up to date. The passing of that bill of rights followed the same pattern but not in the same sequence as we have followed in this debate; the same procedure went on day after day until they arrived at a conclusion; just as we are doing now.
On that occasion each person put forward a particular right that he wanted put in the bill. They were going to bring in a statute that would make these rights law. They had the declaration of rights; but each of these rights had to be confirmed by a convention.
Each person had a particular grievance and a particular right that he wanted to have incorporated in the bill. They had to make a decision quickly, and they set up a committee to put it in concrete form. An individual who had not sat in the house before, by the name of Sommers, was made chairman of this committee. Within four hours he brought in the bill of rights, which was passed in no time.
The same procedure of reporting the bill then took place. They did not take long to pass the bill. Many of the things that have been discussed here today were advanced in the original bill of rights. What we have decided today is no different than what was decided in the original statute of 1689.
We have always marched behind the banner of William III, Prince of Orange, of equal rights to all and special privileges to none; civil and religious liberties. The same bill of rights of 1689 that accomplished so much in

Human Rights
the past for freedom in this dominion of ours will be carried on, and we can still march in the years ahead under the banner of William III, Prince of Orange. Through the years we in this country and other countries have enjoyed the emancipating principles he laid down, clinched and climaxed by blood in the battles of Aughrim, Inniskillen, Derry and the Boyne in 1690. This was followed by the American revolution and the revolution in France, for which he set the pattern.
We have had the advantage of these great principles in the Dominion of Canada and we will now with renewed ardour continue to march behind the emancipating banners of William, Prince of Orange, to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice, who have made this possible with this Canadian bill of rights, for which I extend them my hearty congratulations and thanks in the name of freedom's cause.
