speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in order to bring about the removal of the dilemma referred to by the hon. member for Laurier and the difficulty that will arise through the dissimilarity in the interpretation of the two official languages, I would like to suggest that we will be able to attain that objective by deleting the words, in the English text:
-the provisions of-
The preamble would then read:
And being desirous of enshrining these principles and the human rights and fundamental freedoms derived from them, in a bill of rights which shall reflect the respect of parliament for its constitutional authority-
In the French text you can achieve the same result by the deletion of three words in the twelfth line:
-Ies limites de-

It will then read:
(Translation):
In a bill of rights which shall reflect the respect of parliament for its constitutional authority.
(Text):
We would then achieve, as I see it, the objective which the hon. member had in mind, without having the difficulties that would have arisen through the words "provisions" and "limite", because both words are difficult to translate into the other language. If the Minister of Justice would see fit to do so

I cannot move the amendment myself-I would appreciate it very much.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
If I may, Mr. Chairman, before the Minister of Justice moves the amendment, I would like to draw this to the attention of the Prime Minister. The French text, as I understand it, has one clear meaning, and by eliminating the words that he has suggested my point is that he is weakening the French text.
I was attempting to show the difference between the two, and I would not want to see the French text weakened in any way. I fear that the suggestion of the elimination of these words "les limites de" will substantially restrict the meaning of that text. My feeling is that those words were put in there for a definite purpose, and I am afraid, with all respect to the Prime Minister and his desire to be helpful, that the words suggested will in fact weaken the meaning of the French text.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I could understand that argument if it were not for the fact that this afternoon we accepted the amendment to clause 5, which clearly denotes and determines that the legislative ambit is entirely restricted to those things within the federal jurisdiction.
The preamble was drafted before the amendment to clause 5, which was accepted, as I say, by this committee, and under the circumstances I can see no reason why there will be any misunderstanding. If there had been any doubt before, it was removed by the amendment this afternoon which reads:
That clause 5 be amended by adding thereto the following:
3. The provisions of Part 1 shall be considered as extending only to matters coming within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada.
Following the discussion today we found it possible to arrive at an amendment which would ensure that by no possible interpretation or any other means could it be concluded other than that the bill of rights is exclusively limited to those matters within the federal authority. When the amendment was accepted this afternoon any difference

with regard to the interpretation of the provisions of this bill as might have existed was entirely removed, as I see it.

I have one question to ask about something which has puzzled me for a long time. Is it not possible on a matter of principle to reach an accord as between the English language and the French language? I think we lose a lot of time over misunderstandings as between what is in English and what is in French. Surely, as between French and English principles can be handled.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am certain that that is so, and while I do not claim to be a French scholar I have consulted briefly with some of my colleagues from the province of Quebec and they assure me there will be no difficulty in understanding the words "qui respecte la competence legislative du parle-ment" which says, in other words, a declaration of rights that respects the legislative [DOT]competence of the parliament of Canada, and I have pleasure in moving, seconded by the hon. member for Three Rivers:
That the preamble be amended by deleting "the provisions of" where they appear in line 12 thereof.

I had not intended to say any more on this bill, but having been associated with this matter, as many hon. members have, and knowing every detail of the preamble and the purposes and principles behind it, I must say I cannot accept this proposal. It seems to me that notwithstanding what we did in clause 5 today the situation has not been altered. If the hon. gentleman will recall, when I introduced the amendment to clause 5 I said that notwithstanding the limitations in the preamble of our powers under the constitution it was desirable to restate those limitations in the operative part of the bill for the reason I mentioned, namely the suggestion made by the minister that certain amendments put forward were outside the powers of parliament and that the governing restriction in the preamble did not in any way explain the limitation of powers. Now the preamble is intended to be a reflection of what this bill is, and I suggest to the government that whether they accept the word "limits" or not-I plead with them not to indicate in this preamble that there is no limit to the constitutional authority of this parliament in the matter of human rights and fundamental freedoms.
This bill will pass shortly. It may be the forerunner of a national bill. Let us not give to any province-and there is no reason why we should single out Quebec-the suggestion that we have incorporated in this bill, in its generalization in the preamble, an as-
Human Rights
sertion that there are no limits to the power of the federal parliament in these matters when the law of the land clearly establishes that there are.
This is not a matter of party politics. We have worked together co-operatively to produce a worth-while document. That, I think, parliament has done. Let us not mar that by seeking to take advantage one way or the other. I proposed a word which was not as satisfactory as the phrase "within its competence" but I proposed it because that was the word used in the French text, which gave notice to all and sundry that all we were doing was dealing with matters that came within the powers of parliament under section 91. To say in the preamble, "which shall reflect the respect of parliament for its constitutional authority" does not give notice that there is limitation upon that authority, which there is.
I ask the Minister of Justice in the interest of closing this particular matter with the unanimity that we want to see attached to it, if my word "limitations" is not acceptable let us put some word in that would clearly indicate that we are talking only of matters within our powers. That is the plea I make to the Prime Minister and to the Minister of Justice. They can suggest words which will meet that point. I have no desire not to recognize them as the authors. I simply share with them the desire now to produce a preamble that is going to stand for all time. But let it stand for all time in a way which will not be a false declaration of the condition of affairs under our constitution as between the provinces and the federal government. I do not believe that is an unreasonable request to renew once more.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
With the plea of the hon. member, or, rather, with the thought behind it there must, of course, be complete agreement but I suggest that in our anxiety to see in a draft preamble a positive statement of the limitation on our constitutional authority we did actually insert a phrase which is unnecessary and that is "for the provisions of", or "for the limits of" as the case may be. I agree, of course, it should be made clear both by the provisions of the bill itself and by the preamble that we are acting within the limits of our constitutional authority, but I would suggest to the hon. gentleman that there is no harm and much benefit to be derived from the deletion of these words which are not in conformity as between the English and French text, so the preamble would then read:
-a bill of rights which shall reflect the respect of parliament for its constitutional authority-
Surely it must be agreed that if parliament says we are going to enact a bill of rights

Human Rights
which shall respect our constitutional authority, that means that parliament does not intend and could not intend to go outside the limits of its national authority, because I have never heard any suggestion that the word "respect" means other than that you recognize what it is you are authorized to do. So if you say you are going to have a bill of rights which reflects your respect for your constitutional authority you are saying you are having a bill of rights in which you respect the limits in which you are free to act. We have therefore by the retention of those words made it clear that parliament does not intend to act with disrespect for its authority or with disregard for the limitation which the constitution itself imposes upon it.
Amendment (Mr. Fulton) agreed to: Yeas, 88; nays, 29.

Mr. Chairman, before the
preamble carries I cannot do other than answer the remarks of the Minister of Public Works. I know him well enough to be willing to believe that the hon. gentleman honestly and completely misunderstood what I attempted to say previously. I did not attempt to complain about the acknowledgement of the supremacy of God. What I was complaining about was the inference that exists in the preamble whereby we identify the rule of law with the so-called supremacy of God.
The supremacy of God means many different things to many different Canadians. I believe the hon. gentleman completely misunderstood me in that respect. All authority throughout the ages has always attempted to clothe its authority with the so-called supremacy of God. While I do not advocate opposition to the rule of law I believe the rule of law is not always identical with the supremacy of God as various members of our society may understand that phrase.
I accept the rule of law. I have always attempted to obey the rule of the majority. But let us not be sanctimonious. For a member of the Conservative party and the Conservative government, which government and party have always been willing to worship the economic anarchy we now have, to worship at the altar of individual free enterprise and to take the hide off their fellow-man's back, to accuse a member of this group of belittling the principle of the supremacy of God is an expression of the worst order.
Even in our limited Canadian history there have been many Canadians who have had to suffer as a result of the rule of law which in their opinion was at variance with the supremacy of God as they happened to understand it at that time. I have only to refer to the following minorities in Canada who

in the course of our limited history have had to suffer because of the rule of law as opposed to the supremacy of God as they understood it:	the Doukhobors; Canadians of
Chinese origin who are among the latest victims; the Seventh-Day Adventists; Canadians of Japanese origin; the Mennonites; the Hutterites; the Mormons or members of the church of the Latter Day Saints as they are also known; the Baptists; the Jehovah Witnesses and the Hebrews of Canada. If I had enough time I might draw out from the annals of Canadian history many other minorities who have had to suffer because the rule of law had to prevail.
All I meant to do was warn against an important document as this undoubtedly is identifying the rule of law with the over-all rule of God because the two are not necessarily identical.

Mr. Chairman, I hesitated initially to speak with respect to this particular matter and certainly it is not my intention to launch into an extended debate or to in any way be contentious. However, during the discussions in the special committee at the time the preamble was being considered my friend the hon. member for Bellechasse and I discussed this question and delved into it in some detail to find out precisely where we stood in respect of the matter. Our researches led us to a United States authority, "Bouvier's Law Dictionary" which defines religion as the religion established by Jesus Christ. The explanation states in part:
Christianity is part of the law of the land.
It indicates that Christianity has been judicially declared to be part of the common law of a number of states in the United States and that this practice came from the English law. The explanation continues:
Christianity was pronounced to be part of the common law, in contradistinction to the ecclesiastical law-Christianity is part of the common law, as its root and branch, its majesty and pillar -as much a component part of that law as the government and maintenance of social order.
It is therefore my contention, Mr. Chairman, and I am sure my friend the hon. member for Bellechasse as well as other hon. members of the committee share this view, that we had no other alternative in adopting this particular preamble and accepting it as it is written, but not in the way the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has stated the case.
Preamble as amended agreed to.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am afraid the rather plain language with which an old soldier will introduce the estimates for the Department of National Defence this evening will come somewhat as an anticlimax to the poetic language and heights of oratory with which the committee has been treated during the past two days by many learned members.
In introducing the estimates of my department I wish to point out that they have already undergone lengthy examination in the special committee on defence expenditures. The committee in its early meetings, of which there were eight, examined the expenditures of this department during the year 1958-59 and then in 16 subsequent meetings discussions were related to expenditures which are foreseen for the fiscal year 1960-61. I attended all but one of those meetings and I was given not only an opportunity to explain our policy and the steps which we are taking to implement our defence commitments but also individual members asked many questions relating both to detail and also to the defence policy in general.
At the beginning of our discussions of these estimates I made, with the approval of the committee, statements relating to our general defence policy and commitments to the United Nations, to NATO, to the defence of the North American continent and to the role the department plays in survival operations. Copies of these statements were subsequently printed in booklet form and were made available to all hon. members of the house. An additional booklet was also distributed giving information directly related to the 1960-61 estimates, and copies of this, too, were sent to all hon. members.
It is my opinion that these meetings of the committee were extremely useful and the detailed information which was supplied to the committee and the discussion which took place brought about a better understanding of the role that the three services and the defence research board are playing and of the problems that confront the department in this day of advanced technology and rapid changes in military strategy.
Supply-National Defence
In general, I think it is fair to say that the majority of the members of the committee were in favour of Canada continuing to play her part in the combined military forces of the west which contribute to the deterrent against aggression. This opinion was expressed in the report of the committee in which you find that the first recommendation made by that committee reads as follows, under the heading of NATO-NORAD:
The committee discussed at some length Canada's international defence commitments which are based on the principle of collective security. In particular, it heard evidence concerning the provision of naval, air and ground forces to NATO and air forces to NORAD, and the provision of forces to support the United Nations Organization in the maintenance of peace. Your committee supports these commitments as providing maximum security for the manpower and financial resources contributed.
Then the committee went on to recommend a continued emphasis on the standardization of equipment and the co-ordination of research and development within NATO. With that recommendation I heartily agree. We are endeavouring to assure standardization within NATO, but there are immense difficulties in the way. Each country wishes to provide its own particular type of weapon and each country wishes to support its own industry, a proportion of which is based upon the production of war equipment.
While the committee in general supported these commitments to which I have referred and will refer again, they quite naturally expressed differences of opinion as to how best to carry out the role that has been assigned to the defence forces, and also as to what equipment should be procured. But I think the consensus was that defence was necessary at the present time. Therefore, I wish to express my thanks to the committee, which was ably chaired by the hon. member from London. Members of that committee served faithfully, attending the meetings regularly and without fear expressed their opinions and asked questions. The committee has rendered a valuable work to this House of Commons and I feel that I would again like to express my thanks to all those who served and who helped to frame these various recommendations.
I should also like to assure the committee that these recommendations, of which there are 12 in number, will receive the most careful consideration, not only of my department but also of the government as a whole. Some of these recommendations I shall refer to again in detail in the course of my remarks. Many of them are far-reaching. The last three recommendations which deal with allowances to personnel overseas, design and development personnel and flying by
7522	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence senior officers are details of administration which I can assure the committee will be looked into most carefully.
In view, therefore, of the information which was supplied to the committee and which has also been made available to the members of the house, in continuing my remarks I am going to surmise that the committee is cognizant of the proceedings of the special committee, and with this in mind I shall endeavour to avoid unnecessary repetition, although to illustrate some of the points upon which I wish to lay emphasis I shall quote from time to time from the special committee's report.
Since world war II the great increase in the power of Soviet Russia has changed the very nature of our defence policy. Today there is no sharp line between peace and war; we live in a twilight zone and this is a new condition.
If you will think back to a few years agp you will realize that no one had ever heard of the expression "cold war". Now, in this twilight zone we are endeavouring to find ways by which we can avoid giving an answer to a choice between nuclear war and the end of our civilization or peace under a communist government. I believe ways can be found eventually which will not make it necessary for us to make that choice. I sincerely trust we shall never be forced into making a choice between those two terrible alternatives.
Diplomacy endeavours to solve these problems through such organizations as the United Nations and NATO, through ad hoc meetings such as the recent ill-fated summit conference and the Geneva disarmament conference and through personal visits of heads of states and foreign secretaries. As the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs have said on more than one occasion, Canada is making every endeavour to bring about a lessening of international tensions and to find means of bringing about permanent disarmament. We pursue this quest relentlessly and sincerely hope that our endeavour will be ultimately successful, but recent international events indicate quite clearly that for the time being at least we must continue to maintain the required military strength.
The threat to our national security and, indeed, to the security of the free world is not only military. It is also political, economic and psychological, and to cope successfully with this total threat Canada must have a total strategy within which all elements, the military, the political, the economic and the psychological are closely co-ordinated and in proper balance. This government endeavours to achieve that aim.


The state of a nation's economy has always been a controlling factor in the size and shape of its armed forces. The actual amount of the defence appropriations is regulated by government policy. This is affected by many factors, for example, the actual economic state of the country and the apparent imminence or remoteness of the threat.
Two new factors have arisen in recent years which influence the relationship between finance and defence. In the past early defeats could later be overcome though the process may have been costly in lives, materiel and money. Today the result of a nuclear war will be decided by the forces which exist when the aggressor moves. Should our peacetime forces be inadequate or their armament out of date there will be no opportunity to retrieve the situation after the attack has taken place. The aggressor selects the time for the attack. We can only try to estimate, through the meagre intelligence that we can receive, as to when that time may be. It might be within a few months' time or it may be many years hence. Sometimes, because equipment cannot be obtained just when you want it, it is necessary to take a calculated risk, trusting upon the information that one may receive from various intelligence sources that an attack is not likely within a certain period.
The second major effect on the relationship between finance and defence is the length of time required to produce any new weapon. Therefore, before any new project can be undertaken it is necessary not only to obtain an appropriation for the current year but also commitments for three, four or more years in the future. Expenditures for new equipment are usually quite modest in the first year, perhaps nothing more than preparing the blueprints, but they pyramid very rapidly as production gets under way.
Again, within the last decade entirely new factors have entered into our defence policy and planning. The first is that the primary aim of our defence policy must be to prevent war, not to win a war but to prevent war, and thus the importance placed by the west on their deterrent power. In the past it has sometimes been politically desirable to avoid a war. Today nuclear weapons have created a situation in which the main if not the sole purpose of the armed forces is deterrence. To use our armed forces in action would mean, therefore, that the purpose for which we have kept them has failed.
The second factor is that of collective security. Experience during the past half century has proved that no one country can stand up alone against a powerful aggressor. In military matters Canada is quite incapable of providing everything that would

be necessary lor her defence. Having adopted the principle of collective security we should no longer think in terms of national defence alone but rather of the total defence capabilities of the alliances in which we have joined. We must, therefore, in order to sustain and strengthen these alliances contribute our fair share of the required forces. This I firmly believe Canada is doing not only to the satisfaction of her own conscience but to the satisfaction of our allies.
It is not to be expected that each partner in an alliance should contribute something to each component of the integrated force but rather that national characteristics, national geographic position and national resources should each be used to the best advantage, avoiding as far as possible duplication and overlapping of effort. We do not consider our defence effort in isolation but rather look at the general effectiveness of the alliances to which we are making contributions commensurate with our ability without placing an undue strain upon manpower and financial resources. While the cost of this insurance is heavy I think Canadians as a whole support the commitments we have undertaken.
The third factor is that our armed forces should always be in a much more advanced state of readiness than in the days before the last war. No longer can we rely upon the leisurely mobilization and training of a citizen force. If the armed forces are not ready when war breaks out there will be no opportunity to recover. Never before has it been possible for an aggressor to launch a completely devastating initial attack. There will be no more recovery from any future Dunkirk or any future Pearl Harbor.
These, therefore, are what I consider to be the three guiding principles of our defence policy, the deterrent, collective security and forces in being. They are not always understood, nor are their implementations easy to apply.
For the reasons which I have already given funds are again provided in these estimates to implement the commitments we have undertaken as a government. These are, as I think the committee knows, first of all the provision of naval, air and ground forces for the defence of the Canada-United States region, in other words the North American continent; second, the contribution to the collective defence and the deterrent forces of NATO in Europe and the North Atlantic area; third, the provision of forces to support the United Nations organization in maintaining its peaceful mission.
I should now like to quote from something I said in the committee in connection with this last commitment, that is the provision
79951-0-475
Supply-National Defence of forces to support the United Nations organization in maintaining its peaceful mission. I said in that committee that we maintain in Canada a specially equipped air transportable battalion ready to move anywhere in the world should the need arise. We do maintain that battalion, and that battalion is ready within 48 hours to commence to move to any part of the world. The personnel of the battalion are immunized against tropical and other diseases, and they are organized on a basis of being able to be air transportable, and all their equipment is of a light vehicle nature. The mere fact that they were not required in the present Congo crisis is certainly no reason why we should change our organization in that respect. Under other circumstances this battalion might very easily have been needed. We believe that by maintaining that force we are contributing to what may at some future day be a general international police force, organized and maintained by the United Nations organization. At the present time the United Nations organization has not laid' down to the various countries what their contribution to such an international police force could be, and for that reason, because there is no firm request under normal conditions for a definite unit we also maintain other regular forces in
TTanfd,a if .any further contribution to the United Nations effort is required to prevent the spread of any local war.
Certain personnel in the various corps, particularly the administrative corps, are also immunized against tropical diseases and are maintained at a high standard of readiness so that if the need comes and the United Nations asks for a contribution in any particular case, they are ready. There has been a clear example of that during the last week when a firm request was made from the United Nations organization for certain types of signal personnel and administrative personnel to be made available for the operation of United Nations forces in the Congo.
Then I went on to say in the committee that we attach importance to having forces in being so that they are readily available for these peace-preserving missions. We have announced recently the purchase of various forms of transport aircraft which will greatly increase our capabilities for various missions. I went on to mention the types, the CC-109, a long range transport known as the CC-106, and more recently the purchase of the C-130B, a heavy transport aircraft which can handle even the heaviest equipment in the army. These last named aircraft will not be delivered until later this year, but when we have these new aircraft we will be able to handle, with
7524	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence our own transport, any contingent which we are likely to be asked for by the United Nations to supply.
Under present circumstances we are operating with a limited number of North Stars which are available for transporting forces which are earmarked for the Congo, and also carrying out other normal duties which they have to do, such as supplying the Canadian forces in Indochina, in Palestine and on the Israeli-Egyptian border. They also, of course, maintain the brigade and air division in Europe. I should have said that they assist in the maintenance of the brigade and air division and the transfer of personnel.
Then, more recently, as was announced by the Prime Minister the other day, we have arranged to purchase four of the De Havil-land Caribou aircraft. We have been considering this move for some time, and then this emergency arose. The aircraft has been thoroughly tested and is a remarkable aircraft, unique in its characteristics. No other aircraft in the world is available now which can carry out the functions that the Caribou can. It is able to lift a load of three tons a distance of 500 miles with its ordinary fuel tanks. Larger fuel tanks can be added, which of course will-
The minister said 500 miles; did he not mean 5,000 miles?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
No, 500 miles with its ordinary fuel tanks, a load of three tons. It is capable of taking off with a full load in 500 feet. Now this is just the type of aircraft which will be required to supply the forces which we are sending to the Congo, and which may have to maintain signal links with the various brigade headquarters from the centre at Leopoldville. Many of the airfields in the Congo are in a deteriorating condition owing to the fact that it has not been possible to keep up their maintenance. So I think that gives the committee an idea of the state of readiness in which our forces are so that they may carry out the tasks which they may be asked to perform in support of the United Nations.
These commitments-that is, the defence of the North American continent, the contributions to NATO and the contributions we may make toward the peace-preserving efforts of the United Nations-are all aimed at preventing wars. The operations of the United Nations today in the Congo are aimed at that very purpose of preventing the outspreading of some local war.
The forces of the western nations, whether in NATO, in the United Nations police or


truce forces, or on the North American continent, are contributing to this over-all deterrent against military aggression. If I keep emphasizing the question of deterrent I do so because that is the main purpose of all our defence forces.

I am
afraid I will have to interrupt the minister, because his time has expired.
May I ask that the minister be given all the extended time he wants to make his presentation?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. The success of the deterrent depends upon us. When I say "us" I refer to the members of NATO in particular, although it applies to all peace loving countries throughout the whole world. It depends, therefore, on the fact that we and the other peace loving countries are ready and prepared to resist any act of aggression whether it be a minor incursion or a full scale assault. Forces in being and fully trained are required to ensure that any would-be aggressor knows that immediate action will be taken at the first sign of any such attack.
As Canada's part toward the collective defence we have some 20,000 regular naval personnel, 47,000 army and 51,000 air force personnel. It should be emphasized that as long as we continue to meet our present commitments the strength of our regular forces must be maintained and, I think, at approximately their present strength.
I cannot see any possibility of material reductions in the size of our regular forces if we are to be able to maintain the commitments to which I have previously referred.
The Royal Canadian Navy has more ships at sea than ever before in peacetime. It requires men to man these ships. In its antisubmarine role the effectiveness of the navy has greatly increased with the entry into the service of the St. Laurent and Restigouche class of destroyer escort. Six further improved Restigouche-type escorts are now under construction. These ships are considered by naval authorities in the alliance as outstanding anti-submarine surface vessels. They would, of course, be complemented in the event of an emergency by the various other anti-submarine forces of our allies.
It is interesting to note that the standing committee gave consideration to this matter and reported under paragraph 12 of the report, that they had heard evidence as to the substantial submarine threat and the possibility that some submarines may be capable of mounting missile attacks against this continent. The committee noted that substantial

sums are provided in the estimates to improve the anti-submarine capability of the fleet and anti-submarine air arms of both the Royal Canadian Navy and the R.C.A.F. and stated:
Your committee recommends intensive study of the advantages of acquiring submarines for antisubmarine operations which could also meet the peacetime training requirements of the Royal Canadian Navy.
That study has been continuing for several months now and I hope it will be possible to make a firm recommendation in the not too distant future. In the meantime we do have the services of three Royal Navy submarines which are attached to the Atlantic fleet of the Royal Canadian Navy, and we have recently obtained on loan a submarine from the United States navy for training purposes on the Pacific coast.
Reference was made to the improvement of the anti-submarine capability and I would like to say in this respect that this committee will be interested to learn of the substantial progress that is being made in the improvement of the anti-submarine capability of the fleet through the development of a variable depth sonar at the Atlantic naval research establishment. This device permits sounding instruments to be towed submerged behind our anti-submarine vessels, thus increasing the ability of our ships to detect a submarine at much greater range than heretofore.
The variable depth sonars have been offered by Canada to our NATO allies and I understand arrangements are being made through the armament committee of NATO on a production sharing basis to equip vessels of some of our allies' fleets. H.M.C.S. Crescent is now equipped with the original set and it is expected that full production will start early next year.
The army has in my opinion four roles to fulfil: first, the commitment of a brigade group in Europe and the maintenance of sufficiently trained groups in Canada in order to rotate that brigade. With reference to the brigade, the committee, at resolution 14, reported as follows:
Your committee noted the Canadian brigade group in Europe had been provided with increased fire-power and that sufficient vehicles had been provided to transport all personnel of the brigade.
That was done last year by providing the brigade with wheeled vehicles capable of transporting all the personnel of that brigade. So the brigade may now be referred to as a motorized brigade. Quoting further from the committee report:
The 762 mm. rocket and its launcher-
That is generally known as the Honest John:
79951-0-475J
Supply-National Defence
-are being acquired and provision is made to complete the development of the Bobcat in the 1960-61 estimates.
The Bobcat is an amphibian, armoured, personnel carrier, having various designs which will enable it to carry different types of loads of personnel and their equipment. We expect the final report of the development stage this fall. I hope that if the develoment and the final report show that this is living up to expectations it will be possible to go into production next year.
The committee also recommended giving consideration to the provision of helicopters which would increase the mobility of the brigade. We have that matter under consideration and it is just a question of when funds are to be made available, because I believe that helicopters will certainly increase the effectiveness of that brigade. The committee supports this development to maintain and improve the brigade's mobility and recommend that if the development of the Bobcat is completely successful a decision be taken as soon as practicable with respect to the equipment of the brigade with these vehicles and these helicopters. No one is more anxious than I am to hear the result of the final development of these projects or to see the mobility of our brigade in Germany increase in that respect.
Now the second role that is assigned to the army is the contribution to UNEF, that is, the force on the Israeli-Egyptian border, and other United Nations missions such as Indochina, Palestine and so forth, and the maintenance of a stand-by force on call to meet any further United Nations request.
In connection with the latest request we have had, namely to send personnel to the Congo, I should like to call attention to the fact that Canada has already sent at very short notice 10 fully trained staff officers who are acting on the staff of the general commanding, and, as has already been mentioned in the house, high praise has been given to Colonel Berthiaume who is chief of staff of that force. These personnel are being sent into Africa, in a fever-stricken country where conditions of living are entirely different from those to which they have been accustomed on this continent. Innumerable diseases brought about by a large number of mosquitoes, flies and pests of all sorts are prevalent and therefore I think it would be entirely wrong for Canada to commit her young men to that theatre of operations without taking every care to protect them both by immunizing them against diseases such as cholera, yellow fever, and that sort of thing and also by providing them with the necessary types of clothing so that they will

Supply-National Defence be able to exist in that country instead of becoming casualties.
The third role given to the army is to maintain a force capable of taking action against any possible commando-type raid in the Arctic or elsewhere in Canada. We have three brigade groups stationed across Canada, one in Quebec and' the Atlantic provinces, one in central Canada and one in western Canada. In each of these brigade groups certain personnel are trained to be airborne- and to have experience in living and operating in the Arctic.
The fourth role about which I shall have more to say later is that of having the necessary trained personnel to assist in survival operations in the event that the deterrent to aggression fails. The Royal Canadian Air Force also has important commitments both on this continent and in Europe. As well as maintaining an air lift operation in support of the United Nations, in Europe the first Canadian air division is part of the fourth allied tactical air force. At the request of NATO the government decided to re-equip the eight squadrons now armed with F-86 Sabre aircraft with an aircraft capable of carrying out a strike reconnaissance role. That was the role assigned to our division by the supreme allied commander in Europe.
I do not think the term "strike reconnaissance" is a very good term. It does not really indicate the particular role that our forces have to play. Reconnaissance, yes. They are equipped for carrying out short range reconnaissance. This is not to be interpreted in any way as carrying out what are frequently referred to as spy missions. We have no aircraft capable of carrying out missions of that sort. This is reconnaissance of troops in operation, reconnaissance of the enemy's forces once an attack has started.
So, also, the strike element is far more in the nature of a counter-bombardment element, that is, the enemy has moved, the enemy is carrying out acts of aggression, he is invading part of the NATO territory. Our aircraft would then be employed in order to engage targets of opportunity and centres where communications meet and other targets of a practical nature rather than of a strategic nature as they present themselves. The range of these aircraft is quite limited and they are in every sense a defensive type of aircraft employed in counter-offensive roles. The aircraft selected for this work is the CF-104 which is now being built by Canadair. Much consideration was given before this particular type of aircraft was decided upon, and after we had made that decision I am happy to be able to say that several other NATO countries adopted this

aircraft and are employing it, some of them in air defence roles, other in the strike reconnaissance role that has been given to our forces.
I wonder if the minister would indicate what other countries are using this aircraft in the reconnaissance role.

So much for the air division. On this continent our air force is responsible for the operation and control of the D.E.W. line stations in Canada, the maintenance of the mid-Canada line and the joint maintenance and operation of the Pinetree radar system. Nine squadrons of the CF-100 interceptor aircraft are presently stationed across Canada, complementing United States interceptors and ground to air missiles as a joint defence against the manned bomber.
As has been stated on numerous occasions, the CF-100 will have to be phased out by 1962 as an operational unit. The aircraft has been in operation now for a number of years and is reaching the obsolescent stage. During the discussions in the committee I had the following to say regarding the replacement of this aircraft, and I do not think I can do better than to read what I said there:
At present the CF-100 all-weather fighter is the Canadian contribution to the manned interceptor forces in NORAD. Of the nine squadrons equipped with these aircraft two squadrons each are located at St. Hubert, Ottawa, Bagotville, North Bay and one at Comox. While it is realized that the period of effectiveness of the CF-100 is limited, ho decision with regard to its replacement has been reached yet. However, the R.C.A.F. has investigated various types of aircraft which might be considered should it be decided to re-equip the squadrons in Canada. The realization that such a decision would involve serious financial implications and the knowledge that there are already a considerable number of interceptors in the North American defence complex, coupled with the changing nature of the threat, requires the most careful consideration before a final decision can be reached. There might be some tactical advantage in introducing a more up-to-date interceptor in our Canadian squadrons at this time but whether such a requirement can be given a high enough priority to justify the considerable expense involved is a matter not yet resolved.
The air defence plan for the whole of the North American continent calls for various types of weapons including both manned interceptors and surface to air missiles. But, as I have said before, it may not be necessary for Canada to contribute to all facets of air defence.
The committee recommended that a decision on this matter should be made as soon as possible. I believe I can assure this committee that a decision will be made in the very near future. We have collected a great

deal of material on this subject and I hope we will be able to make a decision very shortly.
The integration of R.C.A.F. personnel into the command and staff structure of NORAD headquarters and at some joint regional and sector headquarters continues. We are really establishing a unified or integrated command between the R.C.A.F. and the United States air force on this continent.
The Royal Canadian Air Force transport command maintains a large fleet of aircraft, as I have said, for the supply and air lifting of service personnel. Air transport command is looking forward to the introduction later this year of its new aircraft, the CC-106's, the CC-109 and the C-130B. In addition, aircraft of the maritime command work in close co-operation with the Royal Canadian Navy anti-submarine forces. The R.C.A.F. also carries out its national and international obligations in search and rescue operations. In connection with the latter in the past year the air force was called upon to organize searches for 36 lost aircraft. In every case the missing aircraft was found and the survivors were rescued from the crash sites. Apart from search operations more than 160 mercy flights were performed to evacuate sick and injured persons to medical facilities.
The air force also maintains a small air support unit for the United Nations emergency force in Egypt. Hon. members will be aware that in recent months R.C.A.F. transport aircraft have played a vital role in various mercy missions and United Nations undertakings.
In March when a severe earthquake struck the city of Agadir in Morocco, North Star aircraft of air transport command flew 6,647 pounds of medical supplies and medical personnel as a Canadian contribution to the distressed people of the area. In May when a series of earthquakes ravished areas of Chile, five North Stars of transport command flew 25 tons of food, shelters and medical supplies and two Canadian army field hospitals to the areas as a Canadian government gift to the Chilean people. These aircraft subsequently remained in Chile and provided 18 shuttle flights between Santiago and various Chilean points transporting evacuees and supplies.
Four North Star aircraft of the R.C.A.F. air transport command have just recently been engaged in flying food totalling 42,000 pounds from Canada to the Belgian Congo. These aircraft were then made available to the United Nations to transport from Pisa,
Supply-National Defence Italy to Leopoldville. Only today it has been announced in the press that Group Captain Carr of the 412th squadron and a team of staff officers have been sent to the Congo where they are organizing the entire transport command of the United Nations force there. These are all young offlcers who have had considerable experience. They have been trained for this particular task and their ability is recognized by the United Nations who have asked for these personnel.
Closer to home, six R.C.A.F. transport aircraft, together with civilian air lines and private companies, combined in the emergency evacuation of women and children from Gagnon, Quebec when a forest fire threatened to get out of control and envelop the town in May of this year. Only at the end of last week a request came from British Columbia for help in connection with the many fires which are raging in that province. We were able to send helicopters and aircraft which rescued some of the firefighters just in the nick of time. They have carried out invaluable work in reconnaissance of the areas which are now being burned and in transporting personnel. That broadly, I think, illustrates the general disposition of our service personnel. Many of these moves were undertaken at very short notice and the personnel were on their way in a matter of a few hours. I believe that indicates that there is really not the confusion and muddling in the Department of National Defence which has sometimes been suggested exists.
I should like to mention various commands under which the forces served. As I said before, the deterrent consists of sea and land forces with the required ground and air support in Europe plus the retaliatory forces consisting in the main of the aircraft and missiles of the United States strategic air command. These two forces complement each other. It has been suggested-I think quite incorrectly-that since the main deterrent is massive retaliation and since Canada does not contribute directly to this retaliation, we should withdraw our forces from NATO and seek for the dissolution of NORAD.
